◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

GroupBy is the most powerful pandas operation. Split data by a key, apply a function to each group, combine results. Most analytical questions are groupby questions: 'avg revenue per region', 'top 5 products per category'.

The Split-Apply-Combine pattern

  • Split: divide data into groups based on some criterion.
  • Apply: run a function on each group (aggregation, transformation, or filter).
  • Combine: merge results back into one structure.
  • Three operation types: aggregate (one value per group), transform (same shape as input), filter (drop or keep entire groups).

Aggregation - one value per group

import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
 "team": ["A", "A", "B", "B", "B", "C"],
 "player": ["Alice", "Bob", "Carol", "Dave", "Eve", "Frank"],
 "points": [25, 30, 18, 22, 28, 15],
 "rebounds": [10, 8, 5, 7, 12, 6],
})

# Average points by team
df.groupby("team")["points"].mean()
# team
# A 27.5
# B 22.7
# C 15.0

# Many aggregations at once - returns a DataFrame
df.groupby("team")[["points", "rebounds"]].mean()

# All numeric columns
df.groupby("team").mean(numeric_only=True)

# Multiple aggregations on multiple columns - .agg()
df.groupby("team").agg(
 avg_points=("points", "mean"),
 max_points=("points", "max"),
 total_rebounds=("rebounds", "sum"),
 n_players=("player", "count"),
)

# Multiple aggs per column with a list
df.groupby("team")["points"].agg(["mean", "max", "min", "count"])

# Different aggs per column
df.groupby("team").agg({
 "points": ["mean", "max"],
 "rebounds": "sum",
})

Group by multiple columns

sales = pd.DataFrame({
 "region": ["East", "East", "West", "West", "East", "West"],
 "product": ["A", "B", "A", "B", "A", "A"],
 "amount": [100, 200, 150, 300, 250, 175],
})

# Two-level grouping
sales.groupby(["region", "product"])["amount"].sum()
# region product
# East A 350
# B 200
# West A 325
# B 300

# Result has a MultiIndex - reset to columns
sales.groupby(["region", "product"], as_index=False)["amount"].sum()
# Returns a flat DataFrame instead

# Or reset_index()
result = sales.groupby(["region", "product"])["amount"].sum().reset_index()

Built-in aggregations

gb = df.groupby("team")["points"]

gb.mean()
gb.sum()
gb.count() # non-null count
gb.size() # row count (incl. nulls)
gb.min(), gb.max()
gb.median()
gb.std(), gb.var()
gb.first(), gb.last()
gb.nth(0) # first row of each group (alternative to first)
gb.nunique() # unique values per group

# Custom aggregation
gb.agg(lambda x: x.max() - x.min()) # range

# Named aggregations (Python 3.7+) - cleanest
df.groupby("team").agg(
 average=("points", "mean"),
 spread=("points", lambda x: x.max() - x.min()),
)

transform - same shape as input

# transform broadcasts result back to original rows
# Useful for "compute group stat, attach to each row"

df["team_avg"] = df.groupby("team")["points"].transform("mean")
df["pct_of_team_avg"] = df["points"] / df["team_avg"]

# Z-score within each group
df["zscore_in_team"] = df.groupby("team")["points"].transform(
 lambda x: (x - x.mean()) / x.std()
)

# Rank within group
df["rank_in_team"] = df.groupby("team")["points"].rank(ascending=False)

# Compare to: aggregate would collapse to one row per team
# Transform keeps all rows but adds group-level info

filter - keep or drop entire groups

# Keep only teams with average > 20
result = df.groupby("team").filter(lambda g: g["points"].mean() > 20)
# Returns rows from teams A and B (their averages are > 20),
# DROPS team C entirely (avg=15)

# Keep only groups with at least 2 members
df.groupby("team").filter(lambda g: len(g) >= 2)

# Keep only top-3 teams by total points
top_teams = (
 df.groupby("team")["points"].sum()
 .nlargest(3).index
)
df[df["team"].isin(top_teams)]

apply - the catch-all

# Top N rows per group
top_2_per_team = (
 df.groupby("team", group_keys=False)
 .apply(lambda g: g.nlargest(2, "points"))
)

# Same with sort_values + head per group (often faster)
top_2 = (
 df.sort_values("points", ascending=False)
 .groupby("team")
 .head(2)
)

# Custom group-level computation
def gini(values):
 """Gini coefficient - inequality metric."""
 sorted_vals = values.sort_values().values
 n = len(sorted_vals)
 cumsum = sorted_vals.cumsum()
 return (2 * (cumsum * range(1, n+1)).sum() / cumsum.sum() - (n+1)) / n

df.groupby("team")["points"].apply(gini)
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

apply is general but slow - it iterates groups in Python. Prefer built-in aggregations (mean, sum) when possible. transform with a string name is also fast. Use apply only when the alternatives don't fit.

Real-world: customer cohort analysis

orders = pd.DataFrame({
 "customer_id": [1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3],
 "order_date": pd.to_datetime(["2024-01-15", "2024-03-01",
 "2024-02-10", "2024-04-05", "2024-05-15",
 "2024-06-01"]),
 "amount": [100, 50, 200, 150, 75, 300],
})

# Cohort = month of first order
orders["cohort"] = orders.groupby("customer_id")["order_date"].transform("min").dt.to_period("M")

# Per-cohort metrics
cohort_summary = orders.groupby("cohort").agg(
 n_customers=("customer_id", "nunique"),
 n_orders=("customer_id", "count"),
 total_revenue=("amount", "sum"),
 avg_order=("amount", "mean"),
)

# Customer lifetime value
clv = orders.groupby("customer_id").agg(
 n_orders=("amount", "count"),
 total_spent=("amount", "sum"),
 first_order=("order_date", "min"),
 last_order=("order_date", "max"),
)
clv["days_active"] = (clv["last_order"] - clv["first_order"]).dt.days

Practice

Given a DataFrame sales with columns region, product, amount: get the top product (by total amount) within each region.

Show solution 
import pandas as pd

# Aggregate to region+product totals
totals = (
 sales.groupby(["region", "product"], as_index=False)["amount"].sum()
)

# For each region, keep the row with max amount
top_per_region = (
 totals.sort_values("amount", ascending=False)
 .drop_duplicates("region", keep="first")
)

# Or with idxmax()
idx = totals.groupby("region")["amount"].idxmax()
top_per_region = totals.loc[idx]

Key terms

GroupBy
Object representing data split by some key.
Aggregation
Reducing each group to a single value (sum, mean, etc.).
Transform
Returns same shape as input - broadcasts group stats back.
Filter
Keeps or drops entire groups based on a predicate.
apply
General group-level function; flexible but slower than built-ins.
Named aggregation
.agg(new_col=("orig_col", "func")) - cleanest syntax.

Exercise form: distinct customers per category — df.groupby("category")["customer_id"].nunique() — nunique counts DISTINCT values inside each group.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Real data lives in multiple tables. Joining customers to orders to products is bread and butter. Pandas merge mirrors SQL JOINs - inner, left, right, outer - and concat stacks DataFrames vertically or horizontally.

Concat - stacking DataFrames

import pandas as pd

# Vertical stacking (axis=0, default) - same columns
jan = pd.DataFrame({"month": "Jan", "sales": [100, 200, 300]})
feb = pd.DataFrame({"month": "Feb", "sales": [150, 250, 350]})

combined = pd.concat([jan, feb])
# Note: index has duplicates - reset if needed
combined = pd.concat([jan, feb], ignore_index=True)

# Horizontal stacking (axis=1) - same number of rows, different columns
df1 = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3]})
df2 = pd.DataFrame({"b": [4, 5, 6]})
pd.concat([df1, df2], axis=1)
# a b
# 0 1 4
# 1 2 5
# 2 3 6

# Many DataFrames at once - more efficient than appending one at a time
files = ["jan.csv", "feb.csv", "mar.csv"]
all_data = pd.concat([pd.read_csv(f) for f in files], ignore_index=True)

Merge - SQL-style joins

customers = pd.DataFrame({
 "cust_id": [1, 2, 3, 4],
 "name": ["Alice", "Bob", "Carol", "Dave"],
})

orders = pd.DataFrame({
 "order_id": [101, 102, 103, 104, 105],
 "cust_id": [1, 1, 2, 3, 5],
 "amount": [100, 50, 200, 150, 300],
})

# Inner join - only matching rows (default)
pd.merge(customers, orders, on="cust_id")
# 4 rows - cust 1 (twice), 2, 3. cust 4 dropped (no orders).
# cust 5 dropped (no customer record).

# Left join - keep all customers, with NaN where no orders
pd.merge(customers, orders, on="cust_id", how="left")
# 5 rows - includes cust 4 with NaN orders

# Right join - keep all orders, NaN where no customer
pd.merge(customers, orders, on="cust_id", how="right")
# Includes the order from cust_id 5 with NaN customer name

# Full outer - keep everything
pd.merge(customers, orders, on="cust_id", how="outer")
# 6 rows - everyone, with NaNs filled in

# Method form - prefer this
customers.merge(orders, on="cust_id", how="left")

Common merge options

# Different column names in each df
left = pd.DataFrame({"customer_id": [1, 2], "name": ["A", "B"]})
right = pd.DataFrame({"cust_id": [1, 2], "amount": [100, 200]})

merged = left.merge(
 right,
 left_on="customer_id",
 right_on="cust_id",
 how="inner",
)

# Merge on multiple columns
df1.merge(df2, on=["region", "product"], how="left")

# Merge on index
df1.merge(df2, left_on="key", right_index=True)
df1.merge(df2, left_index=True, right_index=True)

# Suffixes for overlapping columns
df1.merge(df2, on="key", suffixes=("_left", "_right"))

# Indicator column shows which side had the row
df1.merge(df2, on="key", how="outer", indicator=True)
# Adds "_merge" column with values: left_only, right_only, both
# Useful for debugging joins
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Always check row count after a merge. 1:N joins multiply rows. N:M joins explode them. If your customer table has 10K rows and your orders have 50K, an inner join could yield anywhere from 0 to 50K rows - never 10K * 50K. validate='1:m' in merge enforces relationship type.

join() - shortcut for index-based merges

# join uses the index by default - cleaner for index-based work
df1 = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3]}, index=["x", "y", "z"])
df2 = pd.DataFrame({"b": [10, 20]}, index=["y", "z"])

df1.join(df2) # left join on index
df1.join(df2, how="inner")

# Equivalent merge call:
df1.merge(df2, left_index=True, right_index=True, how="left")

merge_asof - approximate matches by sort key

# Fast nearest-or-prior matching - for time series joins

trades = pd.DataFrame({
 "time": pd.to_datetime(["2024-05-01 10:00:01", "2024-05-01 10:00:05"]),
 "price": [100.5, 100.7],
})

quotes = pd.DataFrame({
 "time": pd.to_datetime(["2024-05-01 10:00:00", "2024-05-01 10:00:03",
 "2024-05-01 10:00:04"]),
 "bid": [100.4, 100.5, 100.6],
})

# For each trade, get the most recent quote BEFORE it
pd.merge_asof(trades.sort_values("time"), quotes.sort_values("time"),
 on="time")

# Within tolerance
pd.merge_asof(trades, quotes, on="time", tolerance=pd.Timedelta("2s"))

Real-world: enriching transactions

# 4 tables: orders, customers, products, regions
orders = pd.read_csv("orders.csv")
customers = pd.read_csv("customers.csv")
products = pd.read_csv("products.csv")
regions = pd.read_csv("regions.csv")

# Join chain - each step on different keys
result = (
 orders
 .merge(customers, on="customer_id", how="left", validate="m:1")
 .merge(products, on="product_id", how="left", validate="m:1")
 .merge(regions, on="region_id", how="left", validate="m:1")
)

# validate="m:1" says: many orders to one customer.
# Pandas will RAISE if a customer_id appears multiple times in customers
# - catches duplicate-key bugs.

# Verify no rows lost / no rows added unexpectedly
assert len(result) == len(orders), "Row count changed!"

# Detect bad joins via indicator
debug = orders.merge(customers, on="customer_id", how="left", indicator=True)
debug["_merge"].value_counts()
# both: 9999 - good
# left_only: 12 - orders with no customer (DATA QUALITY BUG)

Practice

You have customers (cust_id, name, country) and orders (order_id, cust_id, amount). Compute total amount per country, including countries with zero orders.

Show solution 
import pandas as pd

# Left join customers to orders so customers with no orders are kept
merged = customers.merge(orders, on="cust_id", how="left")

# Group and sum - NaN amounts get treated as 0 by sum
country_totals = (
 merged.groupby("country", as_index=False)["amount"]
 .sum()
 .fillna(0) # in case of all-NaN groups
)

# Countries appear even if their customers had no orders

Key terms

concat
Stack DataFrames vertically (axis=0) or horizontally (axis=1).
merge
SQL-style join on shared columns or indexes.
Inner / left / right / outer
Standard SQL join types - which non-matching rows to keep.
1:1, 1:m, m:1, m:m
Cardinality of join keys; validate= catches violations.
merge_asof
Nearest-or-prior match on a sort key (e.g., timestamp joins).
indicator
Adds _merge column showing which side each row came from.

Modernization note: DataFrame.append is removed — replace with pd.concat([df, new_rows], ignore_index=True); collect pieces in a list and concat once for speed.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

The same data can be 'long' (one observation per row) or 'wide' (one observation per row, many measurement columns). Switching between them is fundamental for plotting, modeling, and reporting. Most beginners get stuck on this for weeks.

Long vs wide format

  • Long: each row is one observation. Columns: id, variable, value. Best for analytics, plotting libraries (seaborn, ggplot).
  • Wide: each row is one entity. Columns: id, var1, var2, var3. Best for spreadsheets, certain modeling tasks.
  • pivot: long → wide. melt: wide → long. They're inverse operations.
  • stack/unstack: do similar things but operate on the index (creating MultiIndex layers).

pivot - long to wide

import pandas as pd

# Long format
long = pd.DataFrame({
 "date": ["2024-01", "2024-01", "2024-02", "2024-02"],
 "product": ["A", "B", "A", "B"],
 "sales": [100, 200, 150, 250],
})
# date product sales
# 0 2024-01 A 100
# 1 2024-01 B 200
# 2 2024-02 A 150
# 3 2024-02 B 250

# pivot - reshape so each product becomes a column
wide = long.pivot(index="date", columns="product", values="sales")
# product A B
# date
# 2024-01 100 200
# 2024-02 150 250

# Reset index to flatten
wide = wide.reset_index()
wide.columns.name = None # remove the "product" label

# pivot fails if there are duplicate (index, columns) combinations
# Use pivot_table instead - it aggregates

pivot_table - aggregating wide format

sales = pd.DataFrame({
 "date": ["2024-01", "2024-01", "2024-01", "2024-02"],
 "region": ["East", "West", "East", "East"],
 "product": ["A", "A", "B", "A"],
 "amount": [100, 200, 50, 150],
})

# When index/columns aren't unique, pivot_table aggregates
pivoted = sales.pivot_table(
 index="date",
 columns="region",
 values="amount",
 aggfunc="sum", # default is mean
)
# region East West
# date
# 2024-01 150 200
# 2024-02 150 NaN

# Multiple aggregations
sales.pivot_table(
 index="date",
 columns="region",
 values="amount",
 aggfunc=["sum", "count", "mean"],
)

# Multiple value columns
sales.pivot_table(
 index="region",
 values=["amount", "quantity"],
 aggfunc={"amount": "sum", "quantity": "mean"},
)

# Add row/column totals
sales.pivot_table(
 index="date",
 columns="region",
 values="amount",
 aggfunc="sum",
 margins=True, # adds an "All" row and column
 margins_name="Total",
)

melt - wide to long

wide = pd.DataFrame({
 "name": ["Alice", "Bob"],
 "math": [90, 85],
 "english": [88, 92],
 "science": [95, 80],
})

# Melt - keep "name", unpivot the score columns
long = wide.melt(
 id_vars="name",
 value_vars=["math", "english", "science"],
 var_name="subject",
 value_name="score",
)
# name subject score
# 0 Alice math 90
# 1 Bob math 85
# 2 Alice english 88
# 3 Bob english 92
# 4 Alice science 95
# 5 Bob science 80

# Why melt? Many libraries expect long format:

stack and unstack

Same as pivot/melt but operate on the index, producing/consuming MultiIndex.

df = pd.DataFrame({
 "math": [90, 85],
 "english": [88, 92],
}, index=["Alice", "Bob"])

# stack - move column labels into the index (wide -> long with MultiIndex)
stacked = df.stack()
# Alice math 90
# english 88
# Bob math 85
# english 92

# unstack - reverse
stacked.unstack() # back to original
stacked.unstack(level=0) # unstack the OUTER level (names)
stacked.unstack(level=-1) # default - unstack the LAST (innermost) level

# In modern pandas, .stack(future_stack=True) is recommended
stacked = df.stack(future_stack=True)

Working with MultiIndex

# Result of groupby with multiple keys is often a MultiIndex
sales = pd.DataFrame({
 "region": ["East", "East", "West", "West"],
 "year": [2023, 2024, 2023, 2024],
 "revenue": [100, 150, 200, 250],
})

result = sales.set_index(["region", "year"])
# revenue
# region year
# East 2023 100
# 2024 150
# West 2023 200
# 2024 250

# Selecting from MultiIndex
result.loc["East"] # all East rows
result.loc[("East", 2024)] # specific row
result.loc[("East", 2023):("West", 2023)] # slice

# xs - cross-section, slice across a level
result.xs(2024, level="year") # all regions for 2024

# Flatten back
result = result.reset_index()

After pivot_table or groupby().agg(), you often get MultiIndex columns or rows. To flatten: df.columns = ['_'.join(c).strip('_') for c in df.columns] for tuples like ('amount', 'sum') → 'amount_sum'.

Real-world: time series wide-to-long

# Survey data: one row per respondent, columns for each year
df = pd.DataFrame({
 "respondent": ["R1", "R2", "R3"],
 "score_2022": [3, 4, 5],
 "score_2023": [4, 4, 5],
 "score_2024": [5, 3, 5],
})

# Melt to long format for analysis
long = df.melt(
 id_vars="respondent",
 value_vars=["score_2022", "score_2023", "score_2024"],
 var_name="year",
 value_name="score",
)
long["year"] = long["year"].str.replace("score_", "").astype(int)

# Now we can compute year-over-year change
long = long.sort_values(["respondent", "year"])
long["yoy_change"] = long.groupby("respondent")["score"].diff()

# Or pivot summaries by year
long.pivot_table(index="year", values="score", aggfunc=["mean", "std"])

Long format
One observation per row; columns include id, variable, value.
Wide format

melt
Wide → long; collapse multiple columns into id/variable/value.

Hierarchical index with multiple levels - common after groupby.

Time-aware data is everywhere - sales, clicks, sensor readings. Pandas datetime is rich and fast. Knowing how to parse, slice, resample, and compute deltas saves you from the swamp of string manipulation.

Parsing dates

import pandas as pd

# When reading CSV
df = pd.read_csv("orders.csv", parse_dates=["order_date", "ship_date"])

# After loading
df["date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["date"])

# Custom format - much faster than auto-detect for big files
df["date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["date"], format="%Y-%m-%d")

# Common formats - cheat sheet
# "%Y-%m-%d" 2024-12-25
# "%m/%d/%Y" 12/25/2024 (US)
# "%d/%m/%Y" 25/12/2024 (Europe)
# "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S" 2024-12-25 14:30:00
# "%b %d, %Y" Dec 25, 2024

# Handle errors
pd.to_datetime(df["date"], errors="coerce") # bad strings -> NaT
pd.to_datetime(df["date"], errors="ignore") # leave bad strings alone
pd.to_datetime(df["date"], errors="raise") # default - raise

# Unix timestamps
pd.to_datetime(df["unix_ts"], unit="s") # seconds since epoch
pd.to_datetime(df["unix_ms"], unit="ms") # milliseconds

# Mix of formats - slower but flexible
pd.to_datetime(["2024-01-15", "Jan 16, 2024", "1/17/24"], format="mixed")

Date components - the .dt accessor

df["date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["date"])

# All datetime components live under .dt
df["year"] = df["date"].dt.year
df["month"] = df["date"].dt.month
df["day"] = df["date"].dt.day
df["hour"] = df["date"].dt.hour
df["weekday"] = df["date"].dt.day_name() # Monday, Tuesday, ...
df["dow"] = df["date"].dt.dayofweek # 0=Mon, 6=Sun
df["week"] = df["date"].dt.isocalendar().week
df["quarter"] = df["date"].dt.quarter
df["is_weekend"] = df["date"].dt.dayofweek.isin([5, 6])

# Period - useful for grouping
df["month_period"] = df["date"].dt.to_period("M") # 2024-12
df["quarter_period"] = df["date"].dt.to_period("Q") # 2024Q4

# Format as string
df["date_str"] = df["date"].dt.strftime("%Y-%m-%d")

Filtering by date

# String comparisons work because pandas is smart
df[df["date"] >= "2024-01-01"]
df[(df["date"] >= "2024-01-01") & (df["date"] < "2025-01-01")]

# .between
df[df["date"].between("2024-01-01", "2024-12-31")]

# By components
df[df["date"].dt.year == 2024]
df[df["date"].dt.month == 12]

# Set index to date for slicing
df = df.set_index("date").sort_index()
df.loc["2024-01"] # all of January 2024
df.loc["2024-01":"2024-03"] # Q1 2024 (inclusive)
df.loc["2024-01-15":"2024-01-31"]

Resample - groupby for time series

# Daily data with date index
df = df.set_index("date").sort_index()

# Resample to monthly - sum per month
monthly = df["sales"].resample("M").sum() # M = month end
monthly = df["sales"].resample("MS").sum() # MS = month start

# Common frequencies (offset aliases):
# D daily W weekly
# M month end MS month start
# Q quarter end QS quarter start
# Y year end YS year start
# H hourly T minute (or "min")
# B business day

# Multiple aggregations
df["sales"].resample("W").agg(["sum", "mean", "max"])

# Forward fill - useful for sparse data
df["price"].resample("D").last().ffill() # daily price, fill weekends

# Downsample with custom function
df["sales"].resample("W").apply(lambda x: x.nlargest(3).mean())

# Upsample - increase frequency
daily = df["weekly_metric"].resample("D").interpolate()

Date arithmetic with TimeDelta

now = pd.Timestamp.now()

# Add/subtract durations
tomorrow = now + pd.Timedelta(days=1)
last_week = now - pd.Timedelta(days=7)
in_2_hours = now + pd.Timedelta(hours=2, minutes=30)

# DateOffset - aware of calendar irregularities
last_month = now - pd.DateOffset(months=1) # always one calendar month
last_business_day = now - pd.offsets.BDay() # skip weekends

# Difference between two dates - returns TimeDelta
delta = pd.Timestamp("2024-12-31") - pd.Timestamp("2024-01-01")
delta.days # 365

# In a DataFrame
df["age_days"] = (pd.Timestamp.now() - df["signup_date"]).dt.days
df["hours_since"] = (pd.Timestamp.now() - df["last_login"]).dt.total_seconds() / 3600

# Rolling window - moving averages, sums, etc.
df["sales_7d_avg"] = df["sales"].rolling(window=7).mean()
df["sales_7d_sum"] = df["sales"].rolling(window="7D").sum() # works for irregular dates
df["sales_30d_max"] = df["sales"].rolling(window=30).max()
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Time zones are sneaky. pd.to_datetime creates naive timestamps by default. Use tz_localize('UTC') to mark a timezone, then tz_convert('US/Eastern') to view in another. Mixing naive and aware timestamps in operations raises errors.

Real-world: cohort retention

# orders: customer_id, order_date
orders["order_month"] = orders["order_date"].dt.to_period("M")

# Each customer's first order month = their cohort
orders["cohort"] = orders.groupby("customer_id")["order_month"].transform("min")

# Periods since cohort
orders["months_since_signup"] = (
 (orders["order_month"] - orders["cohort"]).apply(lambda x: x.n)
)

# Retention table: cohort vs months_since
retention = orders.pivot_table(
 index="cohort",
 columns="months_since_signup",
 values="customer_id",
 aggfunc="nunique",
)

# Convert to retention rates
retention_pct = retention.div(retention.iloc[:, 0], axis=0)

Practice

Given df with a daily date column and visits column, compute a 7-day moving average of visits and the day-of-week with the highest average visits.

Show solution 
import pandas as pd

df = df.sort_values("date").set_index("date")

# 7-day moving average
df["visits_7d_avg"] = df["visits"].rolling(7).mean()

# Day-of-week analysis

dow_avg = df.groupby("dow")["visits"].mean().sort_values(ascending=False)
print(f"Best day: {dow_avg.index[0]} with {dow_avg.iloc[0]:.0f} avg visits")

Key terms

Timestamp
Single point in time - pandas equivalent of datetime.
Timedelta
A duration - difference between timestamps.
Period
A span of time at a specific frequency (month, quarter, year).
.dt accessor
Namespace for datetime methods on a Series.
resample
GroupBy for time series - aggregate over time buckets.
rolling
Moving window calculations - rolling mean, sum, etc.

Method chaining lets you express a whole transformation pipeline as one readable expression - no intermediate variables, no df reassignments. Combined with .pipe() for custom functions, it's the most maintainable pandas style.

The chaining style

# Old style - many intermediate variables
df = pd.read_csv("sales.csv")
df = df.dropna(subset=["amount"])
df = df[df["status"] == "shipped"]
df["amount_usd"] = df["amount"] * df["fx_rate"]
df = df.groupby("region").agg(total=("amount_usd", "sum"))
df = df.sort_values("total", ascending=False)
result = df.head(10)

# Chained style - one expression, top-down read
result = (
 pd.read_csv("sales.csv")
 .dropna(subset=["amount"])
 .query("status == 'shipped'")
 .assign(amount_usd=lambda d: d["amount"] * d["fx_rate"])
 .groupby("region", as_index=False)
 .agg(total=("amount_usd", "sum"))
 .sort_values("total", ascending=False)
 .head(10)
)

# Wrap the whole expression in parentheses to allow line breaks

assign() - add columns inline

# Without assign - breaks the chain
df["new_col"] = df["x"] * 2
result = df.groupby("group").mean()

# With assign - keeps the chain going
result = (
 df
 .assign(new_col=lambda d: d["x"] * 2)
 .groupby("group")
 .mean()
)

# Multiple new columns at once
result = df.assign(
 profit=lambda d: d["revenue"] - d["cost"],
 margin=lambda d: (d["revenue"] - d["cost"]) / d["revenue"],
 log_revenue=lambda d: np.log1p(d["revenue"]),
)

# Why lambda d: d["x"] * 2 instead of df["x"] * 2 ?
# - Lambda refers to the CURRENT state of the chain
# - df["x"] uses the original df (before any chain transformations)

# Subtle bug:
df.dropna().assign(scaled=df["x"] / df["x"].max()) # uses ORIGINAL df["x"]
df.dropna().assign(scaled=lambda d: d["x"] / d["x"].max()) # uses dropped df

pipe() - inject custom functions

# pipe lets you put your own functions into a chain

def remove_outliers(df, col, n_std=3):
 """Remove rows where col is > n_std away from mean."""
 mean = df[col].mean()
 std = df[col].std()
 return df[(df[col] - mean).abs() < n_std * std]

result = (
 df
 .dropna()
 .pipe(remove_outliers, col="amount", n_std=3)
 .query("status == 'shipped'")
 .groupby("region")
 .agg(total=("amount", "sum"))
)

# Without pipe, you'd have to break the chain:
clean = df.dropna()
clean = remove_outliers(clean, col="amount", n_std=3)
clean = clean.query(...)
# pipe keeps it readable

# Pipe is also great for unit-testable transformations
def calculate_metrics(df):
 return df.assign(
 margin=lambda d: (d["revenue"] - d["cost"]) / d["revenue"],
 is_profitable=lambda d: d["margin"] > 0.1,
 )

# Now you can:
df.pipe(calculate_metrics)
# AND test calculate_metrics independently with pytest

Common chain patterns

# Top N per group
top_3_per_region = (
 df
 .sort_values(["region", "amount"], ascending=[True, False])
 .groupby("region")
 .head(3)
)

# Compute metrics by group
group_summary = (
 df
 .groupby("category", as_index=False)
 .agg(
 n_items=("id", "count"),
 avg_price=("price", "mean"),
 max_price=("price", "max"),
 )
 .sort_values("n_items", ascending=False)
)

# Filter then transform
recent_top_users = (
 events
 .query("event_date >= '2024-01-01'")
 .groupby("user_id", as_index=False)
 .agg(events=("event_date", "count"))
 .nlargest(100, "events")
)

# Join then aggregate
revenue_per_country = (
 orders
 .merge(customers, on="customer_id", how="left")
 .merge(countries, on="country_code", how="left")
 .groupby("country_name", as_index=False)
 ["amount"].sum()
 .sort_values("amount", ascending=False)
)
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Long chains can be hard to debug because you can't easily inspect intermediate state. When debugging, break the chain at the suspect step and inspect, OR use .pipe(lambda d: (print(d.shape), d)[1]) to log without breaking. Once it works, recombine.

Debugging chains

# Insert pipe steps to log
def log(df, label):
 print(f"{label}: shape={df.shape}, cols={list(df.columns)}")
 return df

result = (
 df
 .pipe(log, "after load")
 .dropna()
 .pipe(log, "after dropna")
 .query("amount > 0")
 .pipe(log, "after filter")
 .groupby("region").sum()
 .pipe(log, "after group")
)

# Or use a helper class for breakpoints in chains
def inspect(df):
 print(df.head())
 print(df.dtypes)
 print(df.shape)
 return df

result = df.pipe(inspect).dropna().pipe(inspect)

When NOT to chain

# Don't chain when you need the intermediate results
# Bad - can't easily reuse the cleaned df
report = (
 pd.read_csv("data.csv").dropna()
 .pipe(my_transform)
 .groupby("x").mean()
 .to_csv("report.csv")
)

# Better when you need the cleaned df elsewhere
clean = pd.read_csv("data.csv").dropna().pipe(my_transform)
clean.to_csv("clean.csv")

report = clean.groupby("x").mean()
report.to_csv("report.csv")

# Rule of thumb: if you'd reference the intermediate value more than once,
# break the chain. If it's a pure one-shot transformation, chain it.

Practice

Refactor this into a single chained expression: 1) read 'orders.csv' 2) drop rows where amount is null 3) filter to status == 'shipped' 4) add a 'year' column from 'order_date' 5) group by year, summing amount 6) sort by year descending.

Show solution 
import pandas as pd

result = (
 pd.read_csv("orders.csv", parse_dates=["order_date"])
 .dropna(subset=["amount"])
 .query("status == 'shipped'")
 .assign(year=lambda d: d["order_date"].dt.year)
 .groupby("year", as_index=False)["amount"].sum()
 .sort_values("year", ascending=False)
)

Key terms

Method chaining
Calling multiple methods sequentially in one expression.
assign()
Add or modify columns mid-chain; takes lambdas referencing current state.
pipe()
Inject custom functions into a chain; first arg is the DataFrame.
Fluent style
Programming style emphasizing chained, readable transformations.

Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) is the first thing you do with any new dataset and the last thing you skip when things go wrong. It catches data quality issues, suggests feature engineering, surfaces relationships, and tells you whether your modeling assumptions are reasonable. The DataCamp Associate Data Scientist exam tests systematic exploration workflow, summary statistics, and visual diagnostics.

The EDA workflow

★ STANDARD EDA STEPS
  1. Load and inspect shape: rows, columns, dtypes
  2. Summary statistics: mean, median, ranges, missing rates
  3. Univariate: distribution of each feature
  4. Bivariate: relationships between features (correlations, scatter plots)
  5. Target analysis: distribution + feature-target relationships
  6. Quality checks: outliers, duplicates, leakage suspects
  7. Document findings: list issues to fix before modeling

Step 1: load and inspect

import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv('customers.csv')

# Shape
print(f"Rows: {len(df):,}, Cols: {df.shape[1]}")

# Sample
df.head() # first 5 rows
df.tail() # last 5
df.sample(10) # random 10

# Schema
df.info()
# Column names, dtypes, non-null counts, memory usage

# Memory check (especially for big data)
df.memory_usage(deep=True).sum() / 1024**2 # MB

# Inspect column types
df.dtypes.value_counts()
# int64 12
# float64 8
# object 5
# datetime64 2

Step 2: summary statistics

# Numeric summary
df.describe()
# Returns count, mean, std, min, 25%, 50%, 75%, max for numeric cols

# Categorical summary
df.describe(include='object')
# count, unique, top, freq

# All columns
df.describe(include='all')

# Per-column quick check
df['age'].describe()
df['age'].value_counts()
df['age'].nunique()
df['age'].quantile([0.01, 0.05, 0.5, 0.95, 0.99]) # see tails

# Find suspicious values
df['age'].min(), df['age'].max()
# age = -1 or age = 999 → likely sentinel for missing

Step 3: missing values

# Counts per column
df.isna().sum().sort_values(ascending=False)

# Rates (often more useful)
(df.isna().mean() * 100).round(1).sort_values(ascending=False)

# Total cells
df.isna().sum().sum()

# Rows with ANY missing
df.isna().any(axis=1).sum()

# Pattern visualization
import seaborn as sns
sns.heatmap(df.isna(), cbar=False, yticklabels=False)
# Reveals patterns — block of missing rows? Column-wide gaps?

# Optional library: missingno
# import missingno as msno
# msno.matrix(df) # missing-value matrix
# msno.bar(df) # bar of non-null counts
# msno.heatmap(df) # correlation of missingness

Step 4: univariate analysis

Numeric distributions

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

# Histogram for each numeric column
df.select_dtypes(include='number').hist(bins=30, figsize=(15, 10))
plt.tight_layout()

# Box plot for outlier detection
df.select_dtypes(include='number').boxplot(figsize=(12, 6), rot=45)

# KDE for smooth distribution
sns.kdeplot(data=df['income'])

# Things to look for:
# - Skewness (right tail → log transform candidate)
# - Bimodality (two peaks → maybe a categorical hiding inside)
# - Outliers (whiskers, isolated points)
# - Unrealistic values (negative ages, future dates)

Categorical distributions

# Bar chart of value counts
df['city'].value_counts().plot(kind='bar')

# Top N + "Other" for high cardinality
top = df['product_category'].value_counts().head(10)
other = df['product_category'].value_counts().iloc[10:].sum()
combined = pd.concat([top, pd.Series([other], index=['Other'])])
combined.plot(kind='barh')

# Cardinality check
for col in df.select_dtypes(include='object'):
 print(f"{col}: {df[col].nunique()} unique values")
# Very-high-cardinality categorical = consider target encoding or hashing

Step 5: bivariate analysis

Numeric-numeric: correlation

import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

corr = df.select_dtypes(include='number').corr()
sns.heatmap(corr, annot=True, cmap='RdBu_r', center=0, fmt='.2f')

# Pairs with |r| > 0.95 likely redundant — pick one
# Pair with target = candidate predictor

# Scatter plot for two specific features
sns.scatterplot(data=df, x='income', y='spend', alpha=0.5)

# Pairplot for all combinations (use on small subsets — slow)
sns.pairplot(df[['age', 'income', 'tenure', 'target']],
 hue='target',
 diag_kind='kde')

Categorical-numeric: group statistics

df.groupby('city')['income'].describe()

# Box plot per group
sns.boxplot(data=df, x='city', y='income')
plt.xticks(rotation=45)

# Violin plot — distribution per group
sns.violinplot(data=df, x='product_tier', y='order_value')

Categorical-categorical: cross-tabs

pd.crosstab(df['city'], df['product_tier'])
pd.crosstab(df['city'], df['product_tier'], normalize='index') # row proportions

# Heatmap visualization
sns.heatmap(pd.crosstab(df['city'], df['product_tier']), annot=True, fmt='d')

Step 6: target analysis

# Classification: class balance
df['churned'].value_counts(normalize=True)
# 0 0.85
# 1 0.15
# → imbalanced — plan accordingly

# Regression: target distribution
sns.histplot(df['price'], bins=50, kde=True)
# Right-skewed → consider log transform

# Target vs each feature (numeric)
for col in numeric_features:
 sns.boxplot(data=df, x='target', y=col)
 plt.show()

# Target vs each feature (categorical)
for col in categorical_features:
 sns.barplot(data=df, x=col, y='target') # avg target per category
 plt.xticks(rotation=45)
 plt.show()

Step 7: quality checks

# Duplicates
df.duplicated().sum()
df[df.duplicated(keep=False)].sort_values(list(df.columns)) # see them

# Drop duplicates
df = df.drop_duplicates()

# Or partial duplicates (same primary key)
df.duplicated(subset=['customer_id', 'order_date']).sum()

# Outlier detection (IQR rule)
def find_outliers(s):
 q1, q3 = s.quantile([0.25, 0.75])
 iqr = q3 - q1
 return s[(s < q1 - 1.5*iqr) | (s > q3 + 1.5*iqr)]

find_outliers(df['income'])

# Constant or near-constant features (low variance → useless)
for col in df.select_dtypes(include='number'):
 if df[col].nunique() < 5:
 print(f"{col}: only {df[col].nunique()} unique values")

# Data leakage suspects:
# - Features computed AFTER the target was known
# - Features that are too good (correlation > 0.95 with target)
# - Identifier columns that uniquely determine the target

Pandas profiling — automated EDA

# Quick-and-dirty automated report
# pip install ydata-profiling
from ydata_profiling import ProfileReport

profile = ProfileReport(df, title="Data Profile", explorative=True)
profile.to_file("eda_report.html")

# Generates a full HTML report:
# - Summary stats per column
# - Distributions
# - Correlations
# - Missing values matrix
# - Common warnings (high cardinality, skewed, etc.)

# Faster alternatives: sweetviz, dtale, ydata-profiling
# Good first pass; don't replace manual EDA

EDA checklist for any new dataset

★ THE 12-POINT CHECKLIST
  1. Shape and dtypes (df.info())
  2. First/last few rows + random sample
  3. Numeric describe()
  4. Categorical describe(include='object')
  5. Missing-value counts and rates
  6. Cardinality of each column
  7. Histograms / boxplots for numeric features
  8. Value-counts for categorical features
  9. Correlation matrix among numerics
  10. Target distribution (class balance or skew)
  11. Feature-target relationships (univariate)
  12. Duplicates, outliers, leakage suspects

Common EDA mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Skipping EDA and going straight to modeling — catches every bug too late
  2. Treating describe() as enough — always plot too
  3. Not checking for sentinel values — -999, "NA" hide as valid data
  4. Ignoring class imbalance — model can be 99% accurate trivially
  5. Forgetting to look at TARGET vs features — finds the strong predictors
  6. Plotting everything raw without log transform — skewed features hide patterns
  7. Not checking duplicates — they inflate model "confidence"
  8. Pairplots on huge datasets — slow; sample first
  9. Trusting automated profilers blindly — they miss domain-specific issues
  10. Doing EDA on the TEST set — leakage; do it on training only
★ ON THE EXAM

"df.info()?" → Schema: column names, dtypes, non-null counts.

"df.describe()?" → Numeric summary (count, mean, std, min, 25%, 50%, 75%, max).

"df.describe(include='all')?" → Includes categorical and numeric.

"Missing rates?" → df.isna().mean().

"Duplicate rows?" → df.duplicated().sum().

"Correlation matrix?" → df.corr(); plot with sns.heatmap.

"Value counts?" → df['col'].value_counts().

"Class imbalance?" → df['target'].value_counts(normalize=True).

"Outlier detection?" → IQR rule (Q1 - 1.5·IQR, Q3 + 1.5·IQR) or boxplot.

"Distribution shape?" → Histogram + KDE.

"Sentinel values?" → -999, "NA", "?", empty strings; convert to NaN first.

"Automated EDA tool?" → ydata-profiling, sweetviz, dtale.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • EDA is the first step on every dataset and a lifesaver when modeling goes wrong
  • Standard flow: shape → summary stats → univariate → bivariate → target analysis → quality checks
  • df.info(), df.describe(), df.head() are the first three commands on every dataset
  • Always check missing values: counts AND rates per column
  • Watch for sentinel values (-999, "NA") — convert to NaN before treating as missing
  • Histograms + boxplots reveal skew, outliers, and unrealistic values
  • Correlation matrix is the workhorse of bivariate numeric analysis
  • For high-cardinality categoricals, plot top 10 + "Other"
  • Target analysis: class balance for classification; skew for regression
  • Feature-target plots highlight strong predictors before modeling
  • Check duplicates, outliers, and leakage suspects before splitting data
  • Automated profilers (ydata-profiling) give a first-pass report — don't replace manual review
  • Do EDA only on TRAINING data — touching test data biases your modeling choices
  • Document findings: list issues to fix, decisions made, and reasoning

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Univariate analysis examines one variable at a time. It tells you the shape, central tendency, spread, and oddities of each column — and what feature engineering or modeling decisions follow. The DataCamp Associate Data Scientist exam tests distribution diagnostics, skewness/kurtosis, and tests for normality.

Numeric variables — central tendency and spread

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

s = df['income']

# Central tendency
s.mean()
s.median() # robust to outliers; preferred for skewed data
s.mode() # most common value(s)

# Spread
s.std() # sample SD
s.var() # variance
s.min(), s.max()
s.max() - s.min() # range
s.quantile([0.25, 0.5, 0.75])
iqr = s.quantile(0.75) - s.quantile(0.25)
s.mad() # mean absolute deviation (deprecated in newer pandas — use stats.median_abs_deviation)

# Coefficient of variation — scale-free
cv = s.std() / s.mean()

# Robust SD via MAD (median absolute deviation)
from scipy.stats import median_abs_deviation
mad = median_abs_deviation(s, scale='normal') # equivalent to SD for normal data

Shape — skewness and kurtosis

SKEWNESS AND KURTOSIS
Skewness: asymmetry of the distribution.
  0 = symmetric; positive = right tail; negative = left tail
  |skew| > 1 = highly skewed; consider log transform

Kurtosis: tailedness.
  0 (excess kurtosis) = normal; positive = heavy tails; negative = light tails
  Pandas uses "excess kurtosis" (normal = 0); some libraries use raw (normal = 3) 
s.skew() # 0 = symmetric
s.kurtosis() # 0 = normal (excess kurtosis)

# Examples:
# Income (right-skewed): skew ≈ +2
# Test scores (left-skewed): skew ≈ -1.5
# Normal distribution: skew ≈ 0, kurt ≈ 0
# Heavy-tailed (returns): kurt > 3 (highly leptokurtic)

# Rough thresholds:
# |skew| < 0.5: roughly symmetric
# 0.5 < |skew| < 1.0: moderately skewed
# |skew| > 1: highly skewed (transform candidate)

Visualizing distributions

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

# Histogram with KDE
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 4))
sns.histplot(s, bins=30, kde=True, ax=ax)

# Box plot — see outliers
sns.boxplot(x=s)

# Violin — distribution shape + outliers
sns.violinplot(x=s)

# Q-Q plot — diagnose normality
from scipy import stats
stats.probplot(s.dropna(), dist='norm', plot=plt)
# Points on the line → normal
# S-curve → heavy or light tails
# Curve → skewed

# All four together for one variable
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(12, 8))
sns.histplot(s, bins=30, kde=True, ax=axes[0, 0]); axes[0, 0].set_title('Histogram')
sns.boxplot(x=s, ax=axes[0, 1]); axes[0, 1].set_title('Box')
sns.violinplot(x=s, ax=axes[1, 0]); axes[1, 0].set_title('Violin')
stats.probplot(s.dropna(), dist='norm', plot=axes[1, 1]); axes[1, 1].set_title('Q-Q')

Normality tests

from scipy import stats

# Shapiro-Wilk — best for small samples (n < 5000)
stat, p = stats.shapiro(s.dropna())
# H₀: data is normal
# p < 0.05 → reject normality

# Kolmogorov-Smirnov — comparing to any distribution
stat, p = stats.kstest(s.dropna(), 'norm', args=(s.mean(), s.std()))

# D'Agostino's K² — based on skewness and kurtosis; works for larger n
stat, p = stats.normaltest(s.dropna())

# Anderson-Darling — sensitive to tails
result = stats.anderson(s.dropna(), dist='norm')

# With large samples, normality tests REJECT for trivial deviations
# Use Q-Q plot as visual guide; tests as confirmation
# Most ML doesn't need normal features — CLT handles aggregates

Categorical variables — value counts and entropy

cat = df['product_category']

# Frequency
cat.value_counts()
cat.value_counts(normalize=True) # proportions
cat.value_counts(dropna=False) # include NaN counts

# Cardinality
cat.nunique()
cat.nunique() / len(df) # fraction unique (1.0 = ID column)

# Top N + others
top_n = cat.value_counts().head(10)

# Entropy — concentration / diversity
from scipy.stats import entropy
ent = entropy(cat.value_counts(normalize=True))
# Higher entropy = more uniform distribution
# Lower entropy = a few categories dominate
# Maximum entropy = log(k) where k = number of categories

Visualizing categorical distributions

import seaborn as sns

# Bar chart
sns.countplot(data=df, x='city', order=df['city'].value_counts().index)
plt.xticks(rotation=45)

# Horizontal bar — better when many categories
df['city'].value_counts().head(20).plot(kind='barh')

# Pie chart — ONLY for < 5 categories
df['city'].value_counts().plot(kind='pie', autopct='%1.1f%%')
# Pie charts are usually inferior to bar charts; consider before using

# Top N + other
top = df['city'].value_counts().head(10)
other = df['city'].value_counts().iloc[10:].sum()
combined = pd.concat([top, pd.Series([other], index=['Other'])])
combined.plot(kind='bar')

Date / time univariate

import pandas as pd

dates = pd.to_datetime(df['order_date'])

# Range
print(f"Start: {dates.min()}")
print(f"End: {dates.max()}")
print(f"Span: {dates.max() - dates.min()}")

# Frequency by year, month, etc.
dates.dt.year.value_counts().sort_index()
dates.dt.dayofweek.value_counts().sort_index() # 0=Mon, 6=Sun
dates.dt.month.value_counts().sort_index()
dates.dt.hour.value_counts().sort_index()

# Time series of daily counts
dates.dt.date.value_counts().sort_index().plot()

# Detect gaps in date ranges
all_dates = pd.date_range(dates.min(), dates.max(), freq='D')
missing_dates = all_dates.difference(dates.dt.normalize().unique())
print(f"Missing dates: {len(missing_dates)}")

Diagnostic table — one row per column

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

def univariate_summary(df):
 """One row per column with diagnostic stats."""
 rows = []
 for col in df.columns:
 s = df[col]
 info = {
 'column': col,
 'dtype': s.dtype,
 'count': s.count(),
 'missing': s.isna().sum(),
 'missing_pct': s.isna().mean() * 100,
 'unique': s.nunique(),
 }
 if s.dtype.kind in 'biufc': # numeric
 info.update({
 'min': s.min(), 'max': s.max(),
 'mean': s.mean(), 'median': s.median(),
 'std': s.std(),
 'skew': s.skew(),
 'kurtosis': s.kurtosis()
 })
 rows.append(info)
 return pd.DataFrame(rows)

summary = univariate_summary(df)
print(summary)
# Quick scan for: high missing, low cardinality, extreme skew/kurtosis

Decisions that follow from univariate analysis

ObservationLikely action
High skew (|skew| > 1)Log or Box-Cox transform
Heavy tails (high kurtosis)Robust scaling; consider winsorizing
Many unique values for low-cardinality intended columnClean/normalize categorical inconsistencies
High cardinality (1000+ categories)Target encoding, hashing, or drop
Bimodal histogramCheck if a categorical is hidden inside
Most values are zeroConsider sparse representation or zero-inflated model
Constant or near-constantDrop (no predictive value)
Q-Q plot far from lineTransform or use non-parametric methods

Common univariate mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Trusting mean on skewed data — median is more representative
  2. Reporting std for non-normal data without context — IQR or MAD is better
  3. Relying on normality tests for big data — they reject trivially
  4. Skipping the Q-Q plot — most informative single diagnostic
  5. Plotting only the histogram — boxplot reveals outliers more clearly
  6. Pie charts for many categories — bar charts almost always better
  7. Forgetting to check date ranges — missing dates / future dates are common bugs
  8. Confusing kurtosis with skewness — kurtosis is tailedness, not asymmetry
  9. Using nunique() == 1 as the only "useless" check — also flag near-constant columns (e.g., 99% one value)
  10. Ignoring NaN in value_counts — default excludes; use dropna=False
★ ON THE EXAM

"Central tendency for skewed data?" → Median, not mean.

"Robust spread measure?" → IQR or MAD.

"Pandas skewness?" → s.skew(); 0 = symmetric.

"Pandas kurtosis?" → s.kurtosis(); 0 = normal (excess kurtosis).

"|skew| > 1?" → Highly skewed; consider log transform.

"Q-Q plot?" → Visual normality check; scipy.stats.probplot.

"Shapiro-Wilk?" → Normality test; H₀: data is normal.

"Category counts?" → s.value_counts(); include NaN with dropna=False.

"Cardinality?" → s.nunique().

"Bimodal histogram?" → Hidden categorical inside; investigate.

"Date range?" → dates.min() to dates.max(); check for gaps.

"Most informative single plot?" → Histogram + boxplot + Q-Q together.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Univariate = one column at a time; first step of EDA
  • Central tendency: mean (sensitive), median (robust)
  • Spread: std (sensitive), IQR / MAD (robust)
  • Shape: skewness (asymmetry), kurtosis (tailedness)
  • |skew| > 1 suggests a log transform
  • Heavy kurtosis suggests outliers; consider robust methods or winsorize
  • Q-Q plot is the most informative normality diagnostic
  • Normality tests over-reject on large samples — use plots instead
  • For categoricals: value_counts, nunique, entropy
  • Pie charts work only for < 5 categories; bar charts otherwise
  • Bimodal distributions often hide a categorical variable
  • Date columns: check range, gaps, and frequency by year/month/day
  • Build a per-column summary table to scan all features quickly
  • Univariate findings drive transform decisions: log, scale, drop, encode
  • Use boxplot, histogram, KDE, and Q-Q together for the full picture

Bivariate analysis examines pairs of variables — feature-feature and feature-target relationships. It surfaces the strongest predictors, redundant columns, and interaction patterns. The DataCamp Associate Data Scientist exam tests scatter plots, correlation matrices, group-by visualizations, and chi-square independence.

Numeric vs numeric — correlation + scatter

import pandas as pd
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Pearson — linear relationships
df.corr()['target'].abs().sort_values(ascending=False)
# Top correlations with the target

# Spearman — monotonic (rank-based)
df.corr(method='spearman')['target'].abs().sort_values(ascending=False)
# Catches non-linear monotonic relationships

# Kendall tau — also rank-based, more robust on small samples
df.corr(method='kendall')

# Scatter plot — the fundamental bivariate visualization
sns.scatterplot(data=df, x='income', y='spend', alpha=0.5)

# With regression line
sns.regplot(data=df, x='income', y='spend')

# Color by category (3-way visualization)
sns.scatterplot(data=df, x='income', y='spend', hue='product_tier', alpha=0.6)

Correlation matrix — find clusters and redundancy

import numpy as np

corr = df.select_dtypes(include='number').corr()

# Heatmap
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 8))
sns.heatmap(corr, annot=True, fmt='.2f', cmap='RdBu_r', center=0,
 vmin=-1, vmax=1, square=True)

# Mask upper triangle for less clutter
mask = np.triu(np.ones_like(corr, dtype=bool))
sns.heatmap(corr, mask=mask, annot=True, cmap='RdBu_r', center=0)

# Find highly correlated PAIRS (redundancy candidates)
def find_correlated(df, threshold=0.9):
 corr = df.corr().abs()
 upper = corr.where(np.triu(np.ones(corr.shape), k=1).astype(bool))
 pairs = []
 for col in upper.columns:
 for idx in upper.index:
 val = upper.loc[idx, col]
 if pd.notna(val) and val > threshold:
 pairs.append((idx, col, val))
 return pd.DataFrame(pairs, columns=['feature_1', 'feature_2', 'correlation'])

find_correlated(df, threshold=0.9)
# Pairs with r > 0.9 — likely redundant; pick one to keep

Numeric vs categorical — group statistics

# Summary per group
df.groupby('product_category')['price'].agg(['count', 'mean', 'median', 'std'])

# Quick visualization
sns.boxplot(data=df, x='product_category', y='price')
plt.xticks(rotation=45)

# Violin — more shape info
sns.violinplot(data=df, x='product_category', y='price')

# Strip with quartile lines
sns.stripplot(data=df, x='product_category', y='price', alpha=0.4, jitter=True)
sns.boxplot(data=df, x='product_category', y='price', showfliers=False, ax=plt.gca())

# Bar with means + error bars
sns.barplot(data=df, x='product_category', y='price', errorbar='ci')

# Test if group means differ — ANOVA
from scipy.stats import f_oneway
groups = [group['price'].values for name, group in df.groupby('product_category')]
f_stat, p = f_oneway(*groups)
print(f"F = {f_stat:.2f}, p = {p:.4f}")
# p < 0.05 → at least one group differs from the rest

Categorical vs categorical — crosstabs and chi-square

from scipy.stats import chi2_contingency

# Contingency table
ct = pd.crosstab(df['city'], df['product_tier'])
print(ct)

# Proportions
ct_prop = pd.crosstab(df['city'], df['product_tier'], normalize='index')
print(ct_prop)
# Each row sums to 1; shows tier distribution within each city

# Visualize
sns.heatmap(ct, annot=True, fmt='d', cmap='viridis')

# Chi-square test of independence
chi2, p, dof, expected = chi2_contingency(ct)
print(f"χ² = {chi2:.2f}, df = {dof}, p = {p:.4f}")
# H₀: city and tier are independent
# p < 0.05 → significantly associated

# Effect size: Cramér's V
n = ct.values.sum()
cramers_v = np.sqrt(chi2 / (n * min(ct.shape) - 1))
print(f"Cramér's V = {cramers_v:.3f}")
# 0 = no association; 1 = perfect; 0.1/0.3/0.5 = small/medium/large

Feature-target analysis — the main goal of bivariate EDA

# For classification: separation per class
# Numeric feature vs binary target
sns.boxplot(data=df, x='churned', y='tenure')
sns.histplot(data=df, x='tenure', hue='churned', element='step', stat='density')

# For categorical feature vs target — bar of mean(target) per category
df.groupby('product_tier')['churned'].mean().sort_values(ascending=False).plot(kind='bar')
plt.ylabel('Churn rate')
plt.title('Churn rate by product tier')

# Mutual information (captures any kind of relationship)
from sklearn.feature_selection import mutual_info_classif, mutual_info_regression

X = df.drop('target', axis=1).select_dtypes(include='number')
y = df['target']

mi = mutual_info_classif(X, y, random_state=42)
mi_series = pd.Series(mi, index=X.columns).sort_values(ascending=False)
print(mi_series.head(10))
# Higher = stronger relationship; works for linear AND non-linear

Pairwise visualization — pairplot and clustermap

import seaborn as sns

# Pairplot — all pairwise scatters + diagonals
sns.pairplot(df[['age', 'income', 'spend', 'target']], hue='target', diag_kind='kde')

# Limit to important columns — pairplot is O(n_features²)

# Cluster map — group similar columns together
sns.clustermap(corr, annot=True, cmap='RdBu_r', center=0)
# Reorders rows/cols by similarity; reveals natural groups of correlated features

# Color sidebar for column types
col_colors = pd.Series(X.dtypes).map({
 'int64': 'red', 'float64': 'blue', 'object': 'green'
})
sns.clustermap(corr, row_colors=col_colors)

Interaction plots

# Does the effect of one feature depend on another?

# Means by combination of factors
sns.pointplot(data=df, x='product_tier', y='churned', hue='region')
# Parallel lines → no interaction
# Crossing or diverging lines → interaction

# Heatmap of mean target by two categoricals
pivot = df.pivot_table(index='product_tier', columns='region', values='churned', aggfunc='mean')
sns.heatmap(pivot, annot=True, fmt='.3f', cmap='coolwarm', center=0.5)

# Quick test for interaction via groupby
df.groupby(['product_tier', 'region'])['churned'].mean().unstack()

Worked example — full bivariate EDA

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Customer churn EDA
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.stats import chi2_contingency, f_oneway

# Step 1: correlation matrix for numeric
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 8))
sns.heatmap(df.select_dtypes(include='number').corr(),
 annot=True, fmt='.2f', cmap='RdBu_r', center=0)
plt.title('Numeric feature correlations')
plt.show()

# Step 2: numeric features vs target
numeric_features = ['age', 'tenure', 'monthly_spend', 'support_tickets']
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(12, 8))
for ax, feat in zip(axes.flat, numeric_features):
 sns.boxplot(data=df, x='churned', y=feat, ax=ax)
 ax.set_title(f'{feat} by churn')

 # ANOVA p-value
 groups = [df[df['churned'] == c][feat].dropna() for c in [0, 1]]
 f, p = f_oneway(*groups)
 ax.set_xlabel(f'churned (ANOVA p = {p:.3f})')
plt.tight_layout()

# Step 3: categorical features vs target
cat_features = ['city', 'product_tier', 'plan_type']
for feat in cat_features:
 # Mean churn rate per category
 rates = df.groupby(feat)['churned'].mean().sort_values(ascending=False)
 rates.plot(kind='bar', figsize=(10, 4))
 plt.title(f'Churn rate by {feat}')
 plt.ylabel('Churn rate')
 plt.show()

 # Chi-square test
 ct = pd.crosstab(df[feat], df['churned'])
 chi2, p, dof, _ = chi2_contingency(ct)
 print(f"{feat}: χ² = {chi2:.1f}, p = {p:.4f}")

# Step 4: top mutual-info features
from sklearn.feature_selection import mutual_info_classif
from sklearn.preprocessing import OrdinalEncoder

X_for_mi = df.drop('churned', axis=1).copy()
# Encode categoricals so MI can use them
for col in X_for_mi.select_dtypes(include='object'):
 X_for_mi[col] = OrdinalEncoder().fit_transform(X_for_mi[[col]])
X_for_mi = X_for_mi.fillna(-1)

mi = mutual_info_classif(X_for_mi, df['churned'], random_state=42)
mi_series = pd.Series(mi, index=X_for_mi.columns).sort_values(ascending=False)
print(mi_series.head(10))
# Top features by MI — candidate predictors regardless of relationship shape

Common bivariate mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Trusting Pearson when the relationship is non-linear — use Spearman or MI
  2. Reading correlation as causation
  3. Forgetting to handle high cardinality categoricals — chi-square test fails with sparse cells
  4. Pairplot on 50+ columns — explodes; select top features first
  5. Comparing means without checking variances — heteroscedastic comparison is misleading
  6. Confidence in p < 0.05 with huge data — practically tiny associations are "significant"
  7. Missing the leakage tell: a feature with |r| > 0.95 with target — probably leakage
  8. Categorical with too many values for chi-square — combine rare categories or use mutual info
  9. Hidden interactions — main effects of A and B may be tiny but the AB interaction huge
  10. Bivariate analysis without missing-value handling — NaN distorts everything
★ ON THE EXAM

"Numeric vs numeric?" → Scatter plot + Pearson/Spearman correlation.

"Pearson vs Spearman?" → Pearson is linear; Spearman is rank-based (monotonic).

"Numeric vs categorical?" → Boxplot per group + ANOVA.

"Categorical vs categorical?" → Crosstab + chi-square + Cramér's V.

"Feature-target with non-linear?" → Mutual information (sklearn).

"Find redundant features?" → Correlation matrix; pairs with |r| > 0.9.

"Pairplot purpose?" → All pairwise scatter plots in one grid.

"Interaction visualization?" → Pointplot with hue, or pivot heatmap.

"Cramér's V?" → Effect size for chi-square; 0=no association, 1=perfect.

"Suspicious very-high correlation with target?" → Possible data leakage.

"Best test for any relationship type?" → Mutual information.

"Big n + tiny correlation significant?" → Statistically yes, practically no.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Bivariate analysis examines pairs of variables to find relationships
  • Numeric-numeric: Pearson (linear), Spearman (monotonic), scatter plot
  • Numeric-categorical: boxplot per group + ANOVA
  • Categorical-categorical: crosstab + chi-square + Cramér's V
  • Mutual information captures any relationship type, including non-linear
  • Correlation matrix surfaces redundant features (|r| > 0.9) and target-correlated features
  • Pearson r is sensitive to outliers; Spearman uses ranks and is robust
  • Feature-target bivariate is the most important kind of EDA — drives feature selection
  • Visualize bivariate relationships before trusting summary numbers (Anscombe's quartet)
  • For class-target visual diagnostics: boxplot, histplot with hue, mean target per category
  • Suspiciously high correlation with the target → suspect data leakage
  • Always check missing values BEFORE bivariate analysis — NaN distorts everything
  • For big data, prefer effect size over p-values (statistical vs practical significance)
  • Interaction plots reveal effects that single-feature analysis misses
  • Clustermap groups correlated features visually — useful for natural groupings

📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

The target variable is the most important column in any supervised learning project. Its distribution determines the metric you'll use, the resampling strategy you'll need, and whether the problem is even feasible. The DataCamp Associate Data Scientist exam tests recognizing class imbalance, target skew, and target-feature relationships.

Classification — class balance

import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Counts
df['target'].value_counts()

# Proportions
df['target'].value_counts(normalize=True)
# 0 0.85
# 1 0.15

# Visualize
df['target'].value_counts().plot(kind='bar')
plt.ylabel('Count')
plt.title('Target class distribution')

# Imbalance ratio
counts = df['target'].value_counts()
ratio = counts.max() / counts.min()
print(f"Imbalance ratio: {ratio:.1f}:1")

Classifying the imbalance

Ratio (majority:minority)SeverityApproach
~50:50 to 65:35BalancedUse accuracy; no special handling
65:35 to 90:10Mildly imbalancedF1, ROC AUC; class_weight='balanced'
90:10 to 99:1Severely imbalancedPR AUC; SMOTE; cost-sensitive learning
More extremeRare eventAnomaly detection; one-class methods

The trivial baseline

# A model that always predicts the majority class gives accuracy = majority proportion
majority_class = df['target'].mode()[0]
trivial_accuracy = (df['target'] == majority_class).mean()
print(f"Trivial accuracy: {trivial_accuracy:.3f}")

# Any model you train MUST beat this — otherwise it's adding nothing

# Examples:
# 50/50 → trivial accuracy 0.50
# 90/10 → trivial accuracy 0.90 (impressive sounding but useless!)
# 99/1 → trivial accuracy 0.99 (model adds zero value if it matches this)

# For imbalanced data, use class_weight='balanced' or resample
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
model = LogisticRegression(class_weight='balanced', max_iter=1000)

Multi-class targets

df['target_3class'].value_counts(normalize=True).sort_index().plot(kind='bar')
plt.ylabel('Proportion')

# Check class entropy — how informative is the class distribution
from scipy.stats import entropy
ent = entropy(df['target_3class'].value_counts(normalize=True))
max_ent = np.log(df['target_3class'].nunique())
print(f"Entropy: {ent:.3f} of max {max_ent:.3f}")

# Diagnose imbalance per class
counts = df['target_3class'].value_counts()
print("Most common:", counts.idxmax())
print("Least common:", counts.idxmin())
print("Imbalance:", counts.max() / counts.min())

Regression — target distribution

import seaborn as sns

# Always plot the target first
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 4))

# Distribution
sns.histplot(df['price'], bins=50, kde=True, ax=axes[0])
axes[0].set_title(f'Distribution (skew={df["price"].skew():.2f})')

# Q-Q plot

axes[1].set_title('Q-Q plot')

axes[2].set_title('Box plot')

df['price'].describe()

Transform decision tree for the target

import numpy as np

# Heavily right-skewed (skew > 1)? Try log transform
df['log_price'] = np.log1p(df['price'])

# Visualize before/after
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4))
sns.histplot(df['price'], bins=50, ax=axes[0])
axes[0].set_title(f'Raw (skew={df["price"].skew():.2f})')

sns.histplot(df['log_price'], bins=50, ax=axes[1])
axes[1].set_title(f'Log (skew={df["log_price"].skew():.2f})')

# Why transform y?
# - Linear models assume normal residuals
# - Skewed y → skewed residuals → bad CI / inferences
# - After log: model predicts log(y); use np.expm1(pred) to invert

# Box-Cox / Yeo-Johnson for automatic best transform
from sklearn.preprocessing import PowerTransformer
pt = PowerTransformer(method='yeo-johnson')
y_transformed = pt.fit_transform(df[['price']])
# Then pt.inverse_transform(predictions) to get back to original scale

# A single huge y value can dominate MSE

# Inspect tails
df.sort_values('price').head(10)
df.sort_values('price', ascending=False).head(10)

# Decide whether they're:
# - Errors (data entry mistakes): remove

Information value (IV) — for binary classification

import numpy as np

# IV measures predictive power of categorical (or binned numeric) features
# Used in credit scoring, churn, and other binary classification problems

def information_value(df, feature, target):
 """Compute IV between feature and binary target."""
 # Bins for numeric features
 if df[feature].dtype.kind in 'biufc':
 df = df.copy()
 df[feature] = pd.qcut(df[feature], q=10, duplicates='drop')

 crosstab = pd.crosstab(df[feature], df[target])
 crosstab.columns = ['non_event', 'event']

 crosstab['p_event'] = crosstab['event'] / crosstab['event'].sum()
 crosstab['p_non_event'] = crosstab['non_event'] / crosstab['non_event'].sum()
 crosstab['woe'] = np.log(crosstab['p_event'] / crosstab['p_non_event'])
 crosstab['iv_part'] = (crosstab['p_event'] - crosstab['p_non_event']) * crosstab['woe']

 return crosstab['iv_part'].sum()

# IV thresholds (credit scoring convention):
# < 0.02: Unhelpful
# 0.02-0.1: Weak predictor
# 0.1-0.3: Medium
# 0.3-0.5: Strong
# > 0.5: Suspiciously strong (possible leakage)

# Compute for all features
features = df.columns.drop('target')
iv_results = {feat: information_value(df, feat, 'target') for feat in features}
pd.Series(iv_results).sort_values(ascending=False).head(15)

Common target-analysis mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Reporting accuracy on imbalanced data — use F1, ROC AUC, PR AUC instead
  2. Not computing the trivial baseline — you don't know if you're adding value
  3. Imputing the target — drop those rows instead
  4. Ignoring target outliers in regression — they dominate MSE
  5. Trying to model heavily skewed target without transforming — linear assumptions break
  6. Forgetting to inverse-transform predictions after log transform
  7. Treating target as numeric when it's ordinal categorical — use ordinal regression
  8. Cross-validating without stratify on imbalanced classification
  9. Computing IV without binning numeric features — IV needs discrete bins
  10. Mistaking an IV > 0.5 for great predictor — often actually data leakage
★ ON THE EXAM

"Class balance check?" → df['target'].value_counts(normalize=True).

"Imbalance ratio?" → max count ÷ min count.

"Trivial baseline?" → Majority-class proportion (= accuracy of always predicting majority).

"Mildly imbalanced metric?" → F1, ROC AUC.

"Severely imbalanced metric?" → PR AUC.

"Sklearn class weighting?" → class_weight='balanced'.

"Skewed regression target?" → Log transform (np.log1p); invert with np.expm1.

"Skewness threshold?" → |skew| > 1 suggests transform.

"Information Value (IV)?" → Credit-scoring measure of predictive power; 0.1-0.3 medium.

"Always plot target?" → Yes, before modeling.

"Drop missing target?" → Always; never impute.

"CV on imbalanced classification?" → StratifiedKFold.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • The target distribution determines the metric, sampling strategy, and feasibility
  • For classification, compute class proportions and imbalance ratio FIRST
  • Always compute the trivial baseline (majority class accuracy)
  • Balanced (50/50): use accuracy; mildly imbalanced: F1 or ROC AUC; severely: PR AUC
  • For severe imbalance, consider SMOTE, class_weight='balanced', or anomaly detection framing
  • For regression, plot histogram + Q-Q + boxplot of the target first
  • |skew| > 1 → consider log or Box-Cox transform
  • After log-transforming y, remember to inverse-transform predictions
  • Outliers in the target dominate MSE — use robust loss (MAE, Huber) if keeping them
  • For classification: plot each feature's distribution per class to see which separate the classes
  • For regression: scatter each feature vs target to see relationship strength and shape
  • For categorical features: bar chart of mean target rate per category
  • Information Value (IV) is a credit-scoring metric for predictor strength
  • IV > 0.5 often means data leakage — investigate before celebrating
  • Always drop rows where the target is missing — never impute the target

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Univariate looks at one variable, bivariate at pairs — multivariate considers many at once. Real datasets have 10-100+ features and the interesting patterns often involve combinations. The DataCamp Associate Data Scientist exam tests multivariate visualization, PCA for exploration, and feature interactions.

Why go beyond pairs

★ MULTIVARIATE PATTERNS

Patterns invisible in univariate or bivariate analysis:

  • Two features each weakly predict the target, but their INTERACTION is strong
  • Three features are individually correlated, but only two add information (collinearity)
  • Clusters exist in 5D space that vanish when collapsed to 2D
  • An outlier in 2D may be perfectly normal in each individual dimension

Color and size encoding in scatter — adding dimensions

)

PCA for visual exploration

Multicollinearity check

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

# Find clusters of correlated features
corr = df.select_dtypes(include='number').corr().abs()

# Find pairs with high correlation
def find_correlated_pairs(corr, threshold=0.9):
 upper = corr.where(np.triu(np.ones(corr.shape), k=1).astype(bool))
 pairs = []
 for c in upper.columns:
 for r in upper.index:
 val = upper.loc[r, c]
 if pd.notna(val) and val > threshold:
 pairs.append((r, c, val))
 return pd.DataFrame(pairs, columns=['f1', 'f2', 'corr'])

high_corr = find_correlated_pairs(corr, 0.9)
print(high_corr)

# Variance Inflation Factor — formal multicollinearity diagnostic
from statsmodels.stats.outliers_influence import variance_inflation_factor

X_for_vif = df.select_dtypes(include='number').dropna()
vif = pd.DataFrame({
 'feature': X_for_vif.columns,
 'VIF': [variance_inflation_factor(X_for_vif.values, i) for i in range(X_for_vif.shape[1])]
})
print(vif.sort_values('VIF', ascending=False))

# VIF interpretation:
# 1 — no collinearity
# 1-5 — moderate
# 5-10 — high; consider removing
# > 10 — severe; one of the features should go

Common multivariate mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Pairplot on 50 features — explodes to 2500 panels
  2. PCA without scaling — largest-variance feature dominates
  3. Trusting t-SNE distances — they don't preserve global structure
  4. Skipping multicollinearity check — leads to unstable linear models
  5. Confusing PCA components with original features — PCs are linear combinations
  6. Ignoring interactions when models are linear — RF/GB handle them; linear doesn't
  7. Treating cluster IDs as ordered — they're arbitrary labels
  8. Comparing cluster IDs across runs — same data → different labels
  9. Using parallel coordinates without scaling — one column dominates visually
  10. Reading too much into t-SNE / UMAP cluster shapes — artifacts of the algorithm
★ ON THE EXAM

"All pairwise in one image?" → sns.pairplot.

"Many features, one observation per line?" → Parallel coordinates.

"Dimensionality reduction for visualization?" → PCA (linear), t-SNE / UMAP (non-linear).

"PCA before what?" → Always scale features first.

"PCA components?" → Linear combinations of original features ordered by variance.

"explained_variance_ratio_?" → Fraction of total variance per PC.

"t-SNE caveat?" → Distances don't preserve global structure; tune perplexity.

"Clustering for exploration?" → KMeans for spherical, DBSCAN for arbitrary shapes.

"Variance Inflation Factor?" → Multicollinearity diagnostic; > 5 is concerning.

"Interaction visualization?" → Faceted lmplot or pointplot with hue.

"Quick feature importance?" → Fit RandomForest, inspect feature_importances_.

"5+ dimensions in one plot?" → Use color, size, shape, AND facets sparingly.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Multivariate analysis examines many features simultaneously — often reveals patterns invisible in pairs
  • Add dimensions to a scatter plot via hue, size, and style (up to 5 vars)
  • Pairplot shows all pairwise scatters + diagonals; limit to top features (O(n²))
  • Parallel coordinates: each row becomes a line connecting feature values; scale first
  • PCA reduces dimensions linearly while preserving variance; always scale before PCA
  • t-SNE / UMAP reveal non-linear cluster structure but distort distances
  • Cluster IDs from k-means or DBSCAN segment the data for further analysis
  • VIF > 5 indicates multicollinearity — drop one of the correlated features
  • For high-cardinality feature sets, fit a quick RandomForest for importance rankings
  • Interaction detection: faceted lmplot or pointplot with hue
  • Tree-based models capture interactions automatically; linear models need explicit interactions
  • Use PCA loadings (components_) to interpret what each PC represents
  • Cluster summaries (mean of each feature per cluster) make segments interpretable
  • Pairplot and PCA together are a strong starter combo for any new dataset
  • Always combine multiple techniques: visual + statistical + model-based

Outlier detection three ways: the IQR rule — keep rows between Q1 − 1.5×IQR and Q3 + 1.5×IQR on the amount column, filter the rest; the z-score — (x − mean) / std, flagging |z| > 3; and sklearn’s IsolationForest — a model-based detector that flags multivariate outliers a single column’s rule would miss.

EDA isn't done until you've communicated what you found. A great EDA produces a clear narrative for stakeholders - what's in the data, what's notable, what to investigate next, what to act on.

What goes in an EDA report

  • Context: what is this dataset, where did it come from, what's the goal?
  • Shape and structure: how many rows/columns? what does each column mean?
  • Quality: missing data, outliers, duplicates, type issues - and how you handled them.
  • Key findings: 3-5 main takeaways with charts to support each.
  • Suspicious patterns: things that need follow-up.
  • Recommendations: what to do next - more data? specific models? data fixes?
  • Audience matters - executive summary differs from technical handoff.

# Good: titles, labels, units, source
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))
sns.scatterplot(data=df, x="age", y="income", hue="segment", alpha=0.6, ax=ax)
ax.set_title("Income by Age, Colored by Segment")

# Translate technical findings to business language

# Bad: "P-value of t-test for income difference between churners and 
# non-churners is 0.003, with Cohen's d of 0.31"

📊 FIGURE — the steps, in order
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

"Garbage in, garbage out" — most failed ML projects fail at data quality, not algorithm choice. Data cleaning is the bulk of real-world data work. The DataCamp Associate Data Scientist exam tests removing duplicates, fixing dtypes, parsing dates, normalizing strings, and handling categorical inconsistencies.

The cleaning checklist

★ DATA CLEANING ORDER
  1. Inspect: understand the raw data first
  2. Fix dtypes: parse dates, convert numerics, normalize strings
  3. Standardize values: trim whitespace, fix case, normalize categories
  4. Drop duplicates after standardization (so spelling diffs don't hide them)
  5. Handle missing: drop, impute, or flag (per ML ch2)
  6. Outlier review: keep or cap or transform
  7. Sanity checks: ranges, dates, references valid
  8. Document: record every change made

Fixing dtypes

import pandas as pd

# Pandas often guesses wrong on load — check df.dtypes after read_csv

# String → numeric
df['price'] = pd.to_numeric(df['price'], errors='coerce')
# errors='coerce' turns unparseable values to NaN
# errors='raise' (default) errors out
# errors='ignore' leaves unchanged

# Cast columns explicitly
df = df.astype({
 'order_id': 'int64',
 'category': 'category', # huge memory savings on repeated strings
 'price': 'float64'
})

# Booleans from strings
df['active'] = df['active'].map({'yes': True, 'no': False, 'y': True, 'n': False})

# Strings → datetime
df['order_date'] = pd.to_datetime(df['order_date'], errors='coerce')
df['order_date'] = pd.to_datetime(df['order_date'], format='%Y-%m-%d')

# Memory check
df.memory_usage(deep=True).sum() / 1024**2 # MB
# Converting object → category often cuts memory by 10x+

String cleaning

import pandas as pd

# Strip whitespace
df['city'] = df['city'].str.strip() # leading/trailing
df['city'] = df['city'].str.replace(r'\s+', ' ', regex=True) # collapse internal

# Case normalization
df['city'] = df['city'].str.lower() # for matching
df['city'] = df['city'].str.title() # "New York" style
df['city'] = df['city'].str.upper() # "NEW YORK"

# Remove special characters
df['phone'] = df['phone'].str.replace(r'\D', '', regex=True) # digits only
df['name'] = df['name'].str.replace(r'[^A-Za-z\s]', '', regex=True)

# Replace specific values
df['city'] = df['city'].replace({
 'NY': 'New York',
 'NYC': 'New York',
 'N.Y.': 'New York',
 'LA': 'Los Angeles',
 'L.A.': 'Los Angeles'
})

# Standardize "missing" indicators
df = df.replace({
 'N/A': pd.NA, 'NA': pd.NA, '': pd.NA, '-': pd.NA, '?': pd.NA,
 'unknown': pd.NA, 'null': pd.NA
})

# Extract parts with regex
df['area_code'] = df['phone'].str.extract(r'(\d{3})')[0]
df['domain'] = df['email'].str.split('@').str[-1]

Dropping duplicates

df.duplicated().sum() # count of duplicate rows
df = df.drop_duplicates() # remove all-column duplicates

# Partial duplicates (same business key)
df = df.drop_duplicates(subset=['customer_id', 'order_date'])

# Keep first/last occurrence
df = df.drop_duplicates(subset='email', keep='first')
df = df.drop_duplicates(subset='email', keep='last')
df = df.drop_duplicates(subset='email', keep=False) # drop ALL with duplicates

# Find duplicates to inspect before dropping
dupes = df[df.duplicated(subset='email', keep=False)].sort_values('email')

# Standardize BEFORE dropping — "Alice@email.com" and "alice@email.com" differ as strings
df['email'] = df['email'].str.lower().str.strip()
df = df.drop_duplicates(subset='email')

Parsing dates

import pandas as pd

# Automatic parsing (pandas guesses)
df['date'] = pd.to_datetime(df['date'])

# Explicit format (much faster and unambiguous)
df['date'] = pd.to_datetime(df['date'], format='%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S')

# Handle errors
df['date'] = pd.to_datetime(df['date'], errors='coerce') # NaT for unparseable

# Mixed formats — slow but flexible
df['date'] = pd.to_datetime(df['date'], format='mixed', errors='coerce')

# Detect invalid dates (after coerce)
df[df['date'].isna()] # rows with unparseable dates

# Range check
df = df[df['date'].between('2020-01-01', '2025-12-31')]
# Drops dates outside expected range — likely data entry errors

# Common format strings
# %Y-%m-%d 2024-03-15
# %m/%d/%Y 03/15/2024
# %d-%b-%Y 15-Mar-2024
# %Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S 2024-03-15 14:30:00

Inconsistent categorical values

df['status'].value_counts()
# active 500
# Active 150
# ACTIVE 5
# active 3
# inactive 200
# Inactive 50

# Standardize
df['status'] = df['status'].str.lower().str.strip()
df['status'].value_counts()
# active 658
# inactive 250

mapping = {
 'activ': 'active',

}
