A technically correct plot can still be useless or misleading. Good visualization is about clarity, honesty, and matching the chart to the audience. The DataCamp Associate Data Scientist exam tests recognizing common design pitfalls and applying best-practice principles.

The data-ink ratio — remove what doesn't help

★ EDWARD TUFTE'S PRINCIPLE

Maximize the ratio of ink that conveys data to ink that doesn't. Remove chartjunk:

  • Heavy gridlines that fight with the data
  • 3D effects on 2D data
  • Decorative backgrounds
  • Redundant labels (e.g., y-axis title + bar labels of the same value)
  • Borders around every element
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 5))
ax.plot(x, y)

# Hide top and right spines
ax.spines['top'].set_visible(False)
ax.spines['right'].set_visible(False)

# Lighter gridlines
ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)

# Lighter axis ticks
ax.tick_params(colors='gray', length=4)

# Compare: default matplotlib vs minimalist style

Honest scales

⚠ AXIS MANIPULATION CHEATS

Some axis choices are common but misleading:

  • Truncated y-axis on bar charts: starting at 80 instead of 0 makes a 2% difference look like 50%
  • Log scale without labeling: linear-looking distance hides orders of magnitude
  • Inconsistent x-axis intervals: irregular spacing distorts trends
  • Dual y-axes with different scales: implies correlation that may not exist

Rules:

  • Bar charts MUST start at 0 (the bar height represents the value)
  • Line charts CAN truncate (slope represents the change rate)
  • Always label log scales clearly
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4))

# Bad: bar chart starts at 95
axes[0].bar(['A', 'B', 'C'], [98, 99, 100])
axes[0].set_ylim(95, 100)
axes[0].set_title('Misleading: difference looks huge')

# Good: bar chart starts at 0
axes[1].bar(['A', 'B', 'C'], [98, 99, 100])
axes[1].set_ylim(0, 110)
axes[1].set_title('Honest: difference is tiny')

Negative to positiveDivergingRdBu_r, coolwarm

import seaborn as sns

# Colorblind-safe categorical (8% of men are colorblind)
sns.set_palette('colorblind')

# DON'T use rainbow (jet) for sequential — perceptually nonlinear
# DO use viridis or mako — perceptually uniform

# Avoid red-green on the same plot (red-green colorblind is most common)
# Use blue-orange instead

# Test your plot in grayscale — if it's still readable, color is supporting (not carrying) the message

Highlight the important

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Highlight one category among many with color
categories = df['region'].unique()
colors = ['lightgray'] * len(categories)
highlight_idx = list(categories).index('North America')
colors[highlight_idx] = '#d62728' # red

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 5))
df.groupby('region')['sales'].sum().sort_values(ascending=True).plot(
 kind='barh', color=colors, ax=ax
)
ax.set_title('North America leads all regions in sales')

# Annotate the key insight
ax.text(0.95, 0.05, f"NA: $1.2M\n+15% YoY",
 transform=ax.transAxes, ha='right', va='bottom', fontsize=12,
 bbox=dict(boxstyle='round', facecolor='white', edgecolor='gray'))

Titles that tell a story

★ DESCRIPTIVE VS ANALYTICAL TITLES

Bad: "Sales by Region" (describes the chart)

Good: "North America revenue grew 15% in Q4, outpacing all other regions" (states the insight)

The descriptive title forces the reader to interpret. The analytical title delivers the message; the chart provides evidence.

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 5))
df['conversion_rate'].plot(ax=ax)

# Two-line title — analytical claim + descriptive subtitle
ax.set_title('Conversion peaked in March then declined', loc='left',
 fontsize=16, fontweight='bold', pad=20)
ax.text(0, 1.02, 'Conversion rate, daily, 2024',
 transform=ax.transAxes, fontsize=10, color='gray')

# Note: matplotlib's set_title centers by default
# loc='left' aligns with the y-axis — more newspaper-like

Direct labeling vs legends

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Legends make the eye dart back and forth
# Direct labels at line ends are easier to read

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 5))
for region in df['region'].unique():
 region_df = df[df['region'] == region]
 line, = ax.plot(region_df['date'], region_df['sales'])
 # Label at the last point
 ax.text(region_df['date'].iloc[-1], region_df['sales'].iloc[-1],
 f' {region}', color=line.get_color(), va='center')

# No legend needed — labels are right there
ax.spines['top'].set_visible(False)
ax.spines['right'].set_visible(False)

Sort categorical bars by value (usually)

# Default alphabetical order is rarely the most informative

# Sort ascending (smallest at top in horizontal bar)
df.groupby('region')['sales'].sum().sort_values().plot(kind='barh')

# Sort descending
df.groupby('region')['sales'].sum().sort_values(ascending=False).plot(kind='barh')
# (then invert axis or use sort_values without ascending=False)

# EXCEPTIONS — keep alphabetical or natural order when:
# - Ordinal data (low/medium/high)
# - Time periods (Mon/Tue/.../Sun)
# - Audience expects a known order (states, brands)

Annotation — guide the reader to the insight

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 5))
df.plot(x='date', y='sales', ax=ax, color='steelblue', legend=False)

# Mark a key event
ax.axvline(x=pd.Timestamp('2024-03-15'), color='red', linestyle='--', alpha=0.5)
ax.annotate(
 'New product launch',
 xy=(pd.Timestamp('2024-03-15'), 1500),
 xytext=(pd.Timestamp('2024-04-01'), 1800),
 arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', color='red'),
 fontsize=10, color='red'
)

# Highlight a region
ax.axvspan(pd.Timestamp('2024-06-01'), pd.Timestamp('2024-06-30'),
 alpha=0.2, color='green')
ax.text(pd.Timestamp('2024-06-15'), ax.get_ylim()[1] * 0.9,
 'Summer promo', ha='center', fontsize=10)

# Add reference horizontal line
ax.axhline(y=1000, color='gray', linestyle=':', alpha=0.5)
ax.text(ax.get_xlim()[1], 1000, 'Target', va='center', color='gray', fontsize=10)

Audience considerations

AudienceStyle
Technical (data team)More density, axis details, statistical tests visible
ExecutiveOne clear takeaway per chart; minimal axis info; analytical title
PrintGrayscale-safe; high resolution (300 dpi); no transparency that won't print well
Web / interactivePlotly / interactive; hover details; responsive sizing

The chart selection cheatsheet

StoryChart
"X is bigger than Y"Bar chart (horizontal if many categories)
"This went up over time"Line chart
"Composition of a whole"Bar; treemap; rarely pie
"X and Y are related"Scatter plot (or hexbin)
"Distribution"Histogram, KDE, box, violin
"Compare distributions across groups"Boxplot or violin with hue
"Pattern in a matrix"Heatmap
"Geographic"Map (folium, plotly, geopandas)
"Flow / hierarchy"Sankey, treemap, network graph

Common visualization mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Truncating bar chart y-axes — exaggerates small differences
  2. Using rainbow / jet colormap — perceptually nonlinear; not colorblind-safe
  3. Pie chart with many slices — bar or treemap instead
  4. Too many lines in one chart — small multiples or highlight one
  5. 3D bars and pies — distort proportions
  6. Dual y-axes when scales aren't truly comparable
  7. Default fonts that fight with the data — use clean sans-serif (Helvetica, Inter, Roboto)
  8. Descriptive titles instead of analytical — wasted real estate
  9. Forgetting to label units — $? %? K? M?
  10. Forgetting accessibility — check colorblind palette and contrast
  11. Chartjunk — gradients, shadows, borders, decorative backgrounds
  12. Saving low-DPI files — pixelated in print and on retina screens; use dpi=150+
★ ON THE EXAM

"Bar chart y-axis?" → Must start at 0.

"Line chart y-axis?" → Can truncate (slope represents change).

"Sequential palette?" → viridis, not rainbow.

"Colorblind-safe?" → Avoid red-green; use blue-orange or named 'colorblind'.

"Composition with > 5 categories?" → Bar or treemap, not pie.

"Highlight one of many?" → All gray, one color.

"Analytical title?" → States the insight, not just the variable names.

"Direct labels?" → At line ends; no legend needed.

"Sort bars?" → By value (usually descending) unless ordered/time data.

"Chartjunk?" → Visual elements that don't convey data; remove.

"Test in grayscale?" → If still readable, color isn't carrying the message.

"Match plot to question?" → Composition → bar/treemap; trend → line; relationship → scatter.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Maximize the data-ink ratio: remove anything that doesn't convey data
  • Hide top and right spines for cleaner plots
  • Bar charts must start at 0; line charts can truncate
  • Use viridis, mako, or YlOrRd for sequential; RdBu_r for diverging
  • Use 'colorblind' palette or blue-orange (not red-green) for accessibility
  • Test in grayscale — if it's still readable, color isn't carrying the message
  • Highlight one category among many with gray + one color
  • Use analytical titles ("X grew 15%") not descriptive ones ("X over time")
  • Direct labels at line ends beat legends for clarity
  • Sort bars by value (descending) unless the data has natural order
  • Annotate key events, peaks, and reference lines
  • Tailor density and complexity to your audience (technical vs executive)
  • Save at dpi=150+ for retina screens; 300 for print
  • Avoid 3D for 2D data, pie charts for many categories, and rainbow colormaps
  • Match plot type to the question being answered — composition, trend, relationship, distribution

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Static charts are great for reports. Interactive charts (zoom, hover, filter) are great for dashboards and exploration. Plotly produces shareable HTML charts that work anywhere - notebooks, web apps, slides.

Plotly Express - the high-level API

# pip install plotly
import plotly.express as px

# Most basic plot - one line
df = px.data.gapminder()
fig = px.scatter(df, x="gdpPercap", y="lifeExp",
 hover_data=["country"])
fig.show()

# With color, size, animation
fig = px.scatter(
 df, x="gdpPercap", y="lifeExp",
 color="continent", size="pop", size_max=60,
 hover_data=["country"],
 animation_frame="year", animation_group="country",
 log_x=True,
 range_y=[25, 90],
)

# Most chart types are one-liners
px.line(df, x="year", y="lifeExp", color="country")
px.bar(df, x="continent", y="pop")
px.histogram(df, x="lifeExp", color="continent")
px.box(df, x="continent", y="lifeExp")
px.violin(df, x="continent", y="lifeExp", box=True)

# Maps
px.choropleth(df, locations="iso_alpha", color="lifeExp",
 hover_name="country", animation_frame="year")
px.scatter_geo(df, locations="iso_alpha", size="pop")
px.scatter_mapbox(df, lat="lat", lon="lng", hover_name="city")

Customizing Plotly figures

fig = px.scatter(df, x="x", y="y", color="category")

# Update layout

 width=800, height=500,
 font=dict(family="Arial", size=12),
)

# Update axes

fig.update_yaxes(type="log", title_font=dict(size=14))

# Update traces

# Add annotations

 x=50, y=50, text="Important point",
 showarrow=True, arrowhead=2,
)

# Add shapes

fig.add_vline(x=50, line_dash="dash", line_color="red")
fig.add_vrect(x0=20, x1=40, fillcolor="yellow", opacity=0.2)

Subplots and dashboards

 subplot_titles=["Plot 1", "Plot 2", "Plot 3", "Plot 4"])

fig.add_trace(go.Bar(x=["a","b","c"], y=[1,4,2]), row=1, col=2)
fig.add_trace(go.Histogram(x=np.random.randn(100)), row=2, col=1)
fig.add_trace(go.Box(y=np.random.randn(100)), row=2, col=2)

fig.update_layout(showlegend=False, height=600)

# Shared axes
fig = make_subplots(rows=2, cols=1, shared_xaxes=True, vertical_spacing=0.05)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=df.index, y=df["price"]), row=1, col=1)
fig.add_trace(go.Bar(x=df.index, y=df["volume"]), row=2, col=1)

Saving and embedding

# Save as static image - need kaleido
# pip install kaleido
fig.write_image("plot.png", width=1200, height=600, scale=2)
fig.write_image("plot.svg")
fig.write_image("plot.pdf")

# Save as interactive HTML

# Show inline (in notebook)

# JSON representation - for sharing or saving

Plotly graph_objects - lower level, more control

import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure()

# Line trace
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
 x=[1, 2, 3, 4],

# Bar
fig.add_trace(go.Bar(x=["A","B","C"], y=[1,4,2], name="Bars"))

# Heatmap
fig.add_trace(go.Heatmap(z=123456, x=["a","b","c"], y=["x","y"]))

fig.show()

Plotly figures get heavy with many points. Subsample large scatter plots (>10K points) - the browser will lag. For huge data, use Datashader to render to an image, then display in Plotly. Always set include_plotlyjs='cdn' in write_html to avoid 3MB files.

📖 DEFINITIONS AT A GLANCE — key terms in this section
TermDefinition
Maximize data-ink ratioevery pixel should convey data; remove decoration.
Show variationdon't hide ranges with averages alone.

Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

A great chart is one a stranger can understand in 5 seconds. Removing chart junk, picking honest axes, choosing perceptually fair colors - these aren't just aesthetics. They're the difference between communicating insight and confusing your audience.

Tufte's principles

  • Maximize data-ink ratio: every pixel should convey data; remove decoration.
  • Avoid chart junk: 3D effects, gradient fills, redundant grids, decorative icons.
  • Use small multiples instead of dual axes or overloaded charts.
  • Show variation: don't hide ranges with averages alone.
  • Annotation > legend when possible - labels next to data are easier to read.

Honest axes

# Bar charts MUST start at zero
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4))

values = [98, 99, 100, 101]
labels = ["A", "B", "C", "D"]

# DECEPTIVE: y-axis 95-101 makes differences look huge
axes[0].bar(labels, values)
axes[0].set_ylim(95, 102)
axes[0].set_title("Misleading: zoomed y-axis")

# HONEST: from zero
axes[1].bar(labels, values)
axes[1].set_ylim(0, 110)
axes[1].set_title("Honest: y-axis from 0")

# Line charts are different - can start anywhere if labeled
# but be careful with implicit zero baseline expectations

Color choices

# 1. Categorical - distinct hues, avoid red+green together (colorblind)
sns.color_palette("colorblind")
sns.color_palette("Set2") # pastel
sns.color_palette("tab10") # default

# 2. Sequential - one hue, light to dark
sns.color_palette("Blues", as_cmap=True)
sns.color_palette("viridis", as_cmap=True) # perceptually uniform

# 3. Diverging - two hues, white at midpoint
sns.color_palette("RdBu_r", as_cmap=True)
sns.color_palette("vlag", as_cmap=True)

# Avoid:
# - Rainbow (jet) - perceptually misleading, not colorblind-friendly
# - Red+green together without other distinguishing features
# - Too many distinct colors (>7) - hard to map to legend

# Test colorblind-friendliness
# pip install colorbrewer
# Or use viridis/plasma/inferno/cividis (all perceptually uniform)

# Print-safe: also works in grayscale
sns.color_palette("gray", n_colors=5)

Annotation over legend when possible

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 5))

x = np.arange(2015, 2025)
companies = {
 "Acme": [100, 120, 145, 170, 195, 220, 240, 260, 280, 300],
 "BetaCo": [90, 95, 110, 125, 140, 155, 170, 180, 195, 210],
 "Gamma": [80, 100, 110, 115, 120, 125, 130, 135, 140, 145],
}

for name, values in companies.items():
 ax.plot(x, values, linewidth=2)
 # Label at the line's end - much easier than legend lookup
 ax.text(x[-1] + 0.1, values[-1], f" {name}",
 va="center", fontsize=11, fontweight="bold")

ax.set_xlim(2015, 2027)
ax.set_title("Revenue by company (USD millions)")
ax.spines["top"].set_visible(False)
ax.spines["right"].set_visible(False)
plt.tight_layout()

Removing chart junk

# Default matplotlib has lots of visual clutter - clean it up

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))
ax.bar(["A", "B", "C", "D"], [10, 25, 18, 7])

# Remove top and right spines
ax.spines["top"].set_visible(False)
ax.spines["right"].set_visible(False)

# Lighter remaining spines
ax.spines["bottom"].set_color("gray")
ax.spines["left"].set_color("gray")

# Subtle gridlines, behind bars
ax.grid(True, axis="y", linestyle="-", alpha=0.3, zorder=0)
ax.set_axisbelow(True)

# Smaller, gray ticks
ax.tick_params(colors="gray", which="both")

# Bigger title, gray subtitle 
ax.set_title("Revenue by category", fontsize=14, fontweight="bold")

# Direct labels on bars (annotation over legend)
for i, v in enumerate([10, 25, 18, 7]):
 ax.text(i, v + 0.5, str(v), ha="center", fontweight="bold")

plt.tight_layout()

Communicating uncertainty

# Always show variation, not just point estimates
import seaborn as sns

# Bar with error bars - mean + 95% CI
sns.barplot(data=tips, x="day", y="tip", errorbar="ci")

# Box - quartiles + outliers
sns.boxplot(data=tips, x="day", y="tip")

# Strip + box - shows raw points AND summary
sns.boxplot(data=tips, x="day", y="tip")
sns.stripplot(data=tips, x="day", y="tip", color="black", alpha=0.4, size=3)

# Line with confidence band
import numpy as np
x = np.linspace(0, 10, 50)
y = np.sin(x) + np.random.randn(50) * 0.2
y_smooth = np.convolve(y, np.ones(5)/5, mode="same")
y_lower = y_smooth - 0.3
y_upper = y_smooth + 0.3

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(x, y_smooth, color="steelblue")
ax.fill_between(x, y_lower, y_upper, alpha=0.3, color="steelblue")
ax.scatter(x, y, color="steelblue", alpha=0.3, s=10)

Choosing scales

# Linear - default, equal increments
ax.set_yscale("linear")

# Log - for data spanning orders of magnitude
ax.set_yscale("log")
# Use when: comparing $100 to $1M, populations from 1K to 100M, etc.

# Symlog - log but handles zero/negatives
ax.set_yscale("symlog", linthresh=10)

# Square root scale (rare but useful for area-like quantities)
ax.set_yscale("function", functions=(np.sqrt, np.square))

# Date axis
import matplotlib.dates as mdates
ax.xaxis.set_major_locator(mdates.MonthLocator(interval=3))
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mdates.DateFormatter("%b %Y"))

# Percent format
import matplotlib.ticker as mtick
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(mtick.PercentFormatter(xmax=1))

# Currency
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(
 mtick.FuncFormatter(lambda x, _: f"${x:,.0f}")
)
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Pie charts confuse comparisons - your eye can't accurately compare angles. Replace with horizontal bars sorted by value. Stacked bar charts make it hard to compare anything except the totals - use grouped bars or small multiples. Avoid 3D charts entirely.

Final polish checklist

# Before declaring a chart "done", check:
# 1. Does the title state the takeaway, not just describe?
# Bad: "Revenue by region"
# Good: "Western region drove 60% of growth"
# 
# 2. Are axis labels clear and include units?
# Bad: "y", "qtr"
# Good: "Revenue ($M)", "Quarter"
# 
# 3. Is the scale honest? Bars from zero?
# 
# 4. Are colors meaningful and accessible?
# 
# 5. Did you remove unnecessary decoration (top/right spines, heavy grids)?
# 
# 6. Is text big enough to read in the medium it'll be shown in?
# Notebooks vs slides vs papers need different sizes
# 
# 7. Did you save as PDF (vector) for print or PNG (raster) for web?
# 
# 8. Does the source/date appear somewhere subtle?
# 
# 9. Can a stranger understand this in 5 seconds?

Practice

Take a default matplotlib bar chart of ['Q1', 'Q2', 'Q3', 'Q4'] with values [100, 150, 130, 200] and improve it: (1) bigger title with insight, (2) zero baseline, (3) value labels on bars, (4) no top/right spines, (5) source citation in corner.

Show solution 
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

quarters = ["Q1", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4"]
revenue = [100, 150, 130, 200]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))
bars = ax.bar(quarters, revenue, color="steelblue", width=0.6)

# Title with takeaway
ax.set_title("Q4 set a record at $200M, doubling Q1 revenue",
 fontsize=14, fontweight="bold", loc="left")

# Zero baseline
ax.set_ylim(0, max(revenue) * 1.15)

# Value labels
for bar, v in zip(bars, revenue):
 ax.text(bar.get_x() + bar.get_width()/2, v + 5,
 f"${v}M", ha="center", fontweight="bold")

# Polish
ax.set_ylabel("Revenue ($M)")
ax.spines["top"].set_visible(False)
ax.spines["right"].set_visible(False)
ax.tick_params(axis="y", colors="gray")
ax.grid(True, axis="y", alpha=0.3)
ax.set_axisbelow(True)

# Source
fig.text(0.99, 0.01, "Source: Internal Finance, May 2024",
 ha="right", fontsize=8, color="gray")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Key terms

Data-ink ratio
Tufte's metric: data ink / total ink. Higher is better.
Chart junk
Visual elements that don't convey data (3D, gradients, decorations).
Perceptually uniform colormap
Equal data steps look like equal color steps (viridis, plasma).
Small multiples
Grid of small charts using same scale - clearer than overloaded charts.
Direct labeling
Labels next to data points instead of separate legend.

First principle: effective data visualization starts with the QUESTION or message — decide what you want the viewer to conclude, then choose the chart that makes that conclusion obvious.

📊 FIGURE — three parts, none optional
🎯 EXAM TIP
Data storytelling combines visuals, narrative context and explicit takeaways — together more powerful than any one alone. The practical version: put the conclusion in the chart title. "Revenue by month" makes the reader do the work; "Revenue fell 12% after the April price change" is the finding, with the chart as its evidence.

📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Means, medians, std, percentiles - the building blocks of every analysis. Knowing when to use which (mean vs median, std vs MAD) is the difference between robust analysis and one that breaks on outliers.

Central tendency and dispersion

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy import stats

x = np.array([2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9])

# Center
np.mean(x) # 5.0 - sensitive to outliers
np.median(x) # 4.5 - robust
stats.mode(x).mode # 4
stats.trim_mean(x, 0.1) # drops 10% each end

# Spread
np.std(x, ddof=1) # sample std
np.var(x, ddof=1) # sample var
stats.iqr(x) # interquartile range - robust
mad = np.median(np.abs(x - np.median(x))) # MAD - very robust

# Pandas - ddof=1 by default
s = pd.Series(x)
s.describe() # 25/50/75/min/max/mean/std

# Choosing:
# Symmetric, no outliers -> mean + std
# Skewed (income) or outliers -> median + IQR

Quantiles, skew, kurtosis

x = np.random.randn(1000)

# Quantiles
np.quantile(x, [0.05, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.95])
stats.percentileofscore(x, 1.5) # what % below 1.5

# Shape
income = np.random.exponential(50000, 1000)
stats.skew(income) # ~2 (right-skewed)
stats.kurtosis(income) # >0 = heavier tails than normal

# Pandas equivalents
s.skew(); s.kurt()

Correlation and covariance

x = np.random.randn(100)
y = 2 * x + np.random.randn(100) * 0.5

# Pearson - linear
r, p = stats.pearsonr(x, y)

# Spearman - rank-based, robust to outliers, captures monotonic
rho, p = stats.spearmanr(x, y)

# Kendall's tau
tau, p = stats.kendalltau(x, y)

# DataFrame
df.corr() # Pearson default
df.corr(method="spearman")
df.cov() # covariance matrix
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Mean alone is dangerous. [1, 2, 3, 4, 200] has mean 42 - represents none of the values. Always compute median and visualize. If mean and median differ a lot, your mean is misleading.

Practice

Compare mean vs median, std vs IQR for an income column with extreme outliers. Which represents typical values?

Show solution 
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

incomes = np.concatenate([
 np.random.normal(50000, 15000, 990),
 np.random.uniform(800_000, 5_000_000, 10)
])

print(f"Mean: ${incomes.mean():,.0f}") # pulled up
print(f"Median: ${np.median(incomes):,.0f}") # robust ~ 50K
print(f"Std: ${incomes.std():,.0f}") # inflated
print(f"IQR: ${stats.iqr(incomes):,.0f}") # robust

# Median + IQR best summarize "typical income"

Key terms

Mean / Median
Arithmetic average vs middle value; median is robust.
Std / Variance
Spread; var = std²; ddof=1 for sample (Bessel's correction).
IQR / MAD
Robust spread measures - prefer over std when outliers present.
Skew / Kurtosis
Asymmetry / tail weight of distribution.
Pearson vs Spearman
Linear vs rank-based correlation; Spearman robust.

Choosing the right summary — a decision guide

The mean is not "the average to always use" — it's one tool with specific failure modes. Income data: one billionaire moves the mean dramatically while the median barely shifts. The decision flow:

Data looks like…CenterSpread
Symmetric, no big outliers (heights, test scores)meanstd
Skewed (income, house prices, wait times)medianIQR
Outlier-contaminated sensor/log datamedian or trimmed meanMAD
Categoricalmodevalue_counts proportions

Reading describe() like a pro

df['price'].describe()
# count    1000        ← missing = original len - count
# mean      142.7
# std        89.3      ← std ≈ mean? often right-skewed
# min         4.0
# 25%        78.0
# 50%       121.0      ← median << mean confirms right skew
# 75%       187.0
# max       950.0      ← max >> 75% + 1.5*IQR → outliers present

Three diagnostics in one glance: (1) mean vs median — a gap means skew, direction of gap = direction of skew; (2) max vs Q3 — a huge jump flags outliers; (3) count vs len(df) — the silent missing-data check.

Why ddof=1 (and when it bites)

np.std(x)           # ddof=0 — POPULATION std (divides by n)
np.std(x, ddof=1)   # SAMPLE std (divides by n-1) ← almost always what you want
pd.Series(x).std()  # pandas defaults to ddof=1 ✓

Dividing by n−1 (Bessel's correction) compensates for the sample mean being closer to the sample than the true mean is. NumPy and pandas DISAGREE on defaults — a classic source of "why don't my numbers match" bugs between scripts.

Correlation: three coefficients, three questions

MethodCapturesUse when
Pearson rLINEAR relationshipBoth variables roughly normal, relationship looks linear
Spearman ρMONOTONIC (any consistently increasing/decreasing)Outliers present, or curved-but-monotonic relationships
Kendall τRank agreementSmall samples, many ties; more robust p-values
⚠ CORRELATION TRAPS

(1) r = 0 does NOT mean "no relationship" — a perfect U-shape has r ≈ 0. Plot first. (2) Correlation ≠ causation — ice cream sales correlate with drownings (both driven by summer). (3) Anscombe's quartet: four datasets with IDENTICAL means, stds, and r, but wildly different shapes. Statistics summarize; plots reveal.

Putting it together — a real EDA snippet

def robust_summary(s):
    return pd.Series({
        'mean': s.mean(), 'median': s.median(),
        'std': s.std(), 'iqr': s.quantile(.75) - s.quantile(.25),
        'skew': s.skew(),
        'pct_missing': s.isna().mean() * 100,
        'n_outliers_iqr': ((s < s.quantile(.25) - 1.5*(s.quantile(.75)-s.quantile(.25))) |
                           (s > s.quantile(.75) + 1.5*(s.quantile(.75)-s.quantile(.25)))).sum()
    })

df[['price', 'qty', 'rating']].apply(robust_summary).T
✓ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Skewed or outlier-heavy data → median + IQR (or MAD), not mean + std
  • mean vs median gap = skew detector; max vs Q3 jump = outlier detector
  • ddof: NumPy defaults to 0, pandas to 1 — know which you're using
  • Pearson = linear, Spearman = monotonic; always plot before trusting r

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Probability is the language of uncertainty. Bayesian reasoning, A/B tests, ML model outputs all rely on probability rules. Knowing P(A|B) ≠ P(B|A) prevents most analytical mistakes.

Core rules

  • P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B) only when independent.
  • P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B).
  • P(A | B) = P(A and B) / P(B).
  • Bayes: P(H|E) = P(E|H)·P(H) / P(E).

Simulation-based probability

import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

# P(at least one 6 in 4 dice rolls)?
rolls = rng.integers(1, 7, size=(100_000, 4))
prob = (rolls == 6).any(axis=1).mean()
print(f"Empirical: {prob:.4f}")
print(f"Analytical: {1 - (5/6)**4:.4f}")

# Birthday paradox
n_trials = 10_000
bdays = rng.integers(1, 366, size=(n_trials, 23))
collisions = np.array([len(set(row)) < 23 for row in bdays])
print(f"P(collision in 23): {collisions.mean():.3f}") # ~0.51

Bayes' theorem in practice

# Disease screening
# 1% of pop has disease. Test sensitivity 99%, specificity 95%.
# You test positive. P(disease)?

prior = 0.01
sens = 0.99 # P(+ | D)
spec = 0.95 # P(- | no D)
fpr = 1 - spec # 0.05

p_pos = sens * prior + fpr * (1 - prior)
p_d_given_pos = sens * prior / p_pos
print(f"P(disease | +) = {p_d_given_pos:.3f}")
# Just 16.7%! Even a "very accurate" test produces mostly false positives
# when the base rate is low.
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Don't conflate P(A | B) with P(B | A). "Most disease patients tested positive" ≠ "most positive testers have the disease". This is the prosecutor's fallacy - it depends entirely on the base rate.

Combinatorics and expected value

from math import comb, perm, factorial

comb(52, 5) # combos of 5 cards from 52
perm(10, 3) # permutations of 3 from 10
factorial(5)

# P(royal flush) = 4 / C(52, 5)
print(f"{4 / comb(52, 5):.2e}")

# Expected value
# Lottery: $2/ticket, 1/300M to win $1M, 1/1M to win $10K
ev = (1_000_000 * 1/300_000_000 +
 10_000 * 1/1_000_000 +
 0 - 2)
print(f"EV: ${ev:.2f}") # negative

# Linearity: E[X+Y] = E[X] + E[Y] always
# Var(X+Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) only if independent

Practice

Factory A makes 70% (3% defect), B makes 30% (6% defect). A widget is defective. P(came from B)?

Show solution 
p_a, p_b = 0.7, 0.3
p_def_a, p_def_b = 0.03, 0.06

p_def = p_def_a * p_a + p_def_b * p_b
p_b_given_def = p_def_b * p_b / p_def
print(f"{p_b_given_def:.4f}") # 0.4615
# B's share of defects is 46% even though it's 30% of production

Key terms

Conditional probability
P(A|B) = P(A and B) / P(B).
Bayes' theorem
Updates prior using new evidence.
Independence
P(A and B) = P(A)P(B).
Base rate
Prior probability; ignored at your peril.
Expected value
Sum of outcomes weighted by their probabilities.

The vocabulary that unlocks everything else

Probability has four terms that appear in every ML paper, every A/B test, every Bayes discussion. Get these solid and the rest follows:

TermNotationPlain English
JointP(A, B)Both happen
ConditionalP(A | B)A happens, GIVEN we know B happened
MarginalP(A)A happens, ignoring everything else
IndependenceP(A,B) = P(A)P(B)Knowing B tells you nothing about A

Bayes' theorem — worked all the way through

A disease affects 1% of people. A test catches 95% of cases (sensitivity) but false-alarms on 5% of healthy people. You test positive. What's the chance you're sick?

P(sick) = 0.01          # prior
P(+|sick) = 0.95        # sensitivity
P(+|healthy) = 0.05     # false positive rate

# Bayes: P(sick|+) = P(+|sick) * P(sick) / P(+)
# P(+) = P(+|sick)P(sick) + P(+|healthy)P(healthy)
p_pos = 0.95*0.01 + 0.05*0.99      # = 0.059
p_sick_given_pos = (0.95*0.01) / p_pos
print(p_sick_given_pos)             # 0.161 — only 16%!

Why so low? The disease is rare. Among 10,000 people: ~100 sick (95 test +) and ~9,900 healthy (495 test + falsely). Of 590 positives, only 95 are real — 16%. The prior dominates when the base rate is extreme. This is why doctors retest, and why fraud models with 99% accuracy can still be useless.

💡 THE COUNT TRICK

Confused by Bayes? Convert to counts of 10,000 imaginary people and tally the four groups (sick+, sick−, healthy+, healthy−). The formula becomes obvious arithmetic.

Simulation: when math gets hard, sample

import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

# Birthday problem: P(shared birthday among 23 people)?
trials = 100_000
hits = 0
for _ in range(trials):
    bdays = rng.integers(0, 365, size=23)
    if len(np.unique(bdays)) < 23:
        hits += 1
print(hits / trials)   # ≈ 0.507 — the famous result

# Monte Carlo is the data scientist's superpower:
# any probability you can SIMULATE, you can ESTIMATE.

Expected value — the decision-making tool

# A game: pay $5 to roll a die; win $20 on a six.
ev = (-5) + (1/6) * 20      # = -1.67 → losing game, don't play

# Business version: send a $2 coupon; 8% convert at $30 profit
ev_coupon = -2 + 0.08 * 30  # = +0.40 per coupon → send them

EV thinking turns vague "should we?" debates into arithmetic. Combine with simulation for complex cases (varying conversion rates, segment differences).

⚠ INDEPENDENCE IS AN ASSUMPTION

Multiplying probabilities (P(A)·P(B)) requires independence. Real-world events are often correlated: loan defaults cluster in recessions; server failures share power supplies. Assuming independence when it's false is how 2008-style risk models blew up.

✓ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • P(A|B) ≠ P(B|A) — confusing them is the prosecutor's fallacy
  • Bayes with rare events: the prior dominates; convert to counts when confused
  • Monte Carlo simulation estimates any probability you can code
  • Expected value turns decisions into arithmetic — but check independence assumptions

Exercise form: one random float in [0, 1) — random.random(); for a range use random.uniform(a, b).

Distributions describe how random outcomes are spread. Normal for measurement noise, Poisson for counts, Binomial for trials. Recognizing the right one tells you what model and test to use.

Continuous distributions

import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

# Normal (Gaussian)
samples = stats.norm.rvs(loc=100, scale=15, size=1000)
stats.norm.cdf(85, loc=100, scale=15) # P(IQ <= 85)
stats.norm.ppf(0.975, loc=100, scale=15) # 97.5th percentile

# Exponential - waiting times
stats.expon.rvs(scale=0.5, size=1000)
stats.expon.cdf(1.0, scale=0.5)

# t-distribution - heavy tails
stats.t.rvs(df=3, size=1000) # heavy
stats.t.rvs(df=30, size=1000) # near normal

# Beta - bounded [0, 1]
stats.beta.rvs(a=2, b=5, size=1000)

# Gamma - generalizes exponential
stats.gamma.rvs(a=2, scale=2, size=1000)

Discrete distributions

# Binomial - n trials, prob p of success
stats.binom.pmf(7, n=10, p=0.5) # exactly 7 heads
stats.binom.cdf(7, n=10, p=0.5) # at most 7
# Mean = np, Var = np(1-p)

# Poisson - count of rare events
stats.poisson.pmf(5, mu=3.5) # exactly 5 in interval
stats.poisson.cdf(2, mu=3.5) # 0, 1, or 2 events
# Mean = Var = mu

# Geometric - trials to first success
stats.geom.pmf(3, p=0.5)

# Negative binomial - trials to k-th success
# Multinomial - generalization to >2 outcomes

Fitting and goodness-of-fit

data = stats.norm.rvs(loc=50, scale=10, size=1000)

# MLE fit
mean, std = stats.norm.fit(data)

# Visual + Q-Q plot
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4))
ax[0].hist(data, bins=30, density=True, alpha=0.6)
x = np.linspace(data.min(), data.max(), 100)
ax[0].plot(x, stats.norm.pdf(x, mean, std), 'r-')
stats.probplot(data, dist=stats.norm, plot=ax[1])

# K-S test for goodness-of-fit
ks_stat, p = stats.kstest(data, "norm", args=(mean, std))
# Low p -> data is NOT from this distribution

Recognizing distributions

  • Heights, IQ, measurement errors -> Normal (CLT in action).
  • Income, file sizes, populations -> Log-normal or Pareto (heavy right tail).
  • Counts of rare events -> Poisson.
  • Time between events -> Exponential.
  • Bounded proportions -> Beta.
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Real data rarely fits any standard distribution exactly. Use these as approximations and validate with Q-Q plots / K-S. Many ML methods tolerate moderate violations of normality, but tail-sensitive methods (CIs, anomaly detection) don't.

Practice

Website gets ~2 clicks/min on average. (a) P(exactly 5 in 1 min)? (b) P(>10 in 5 min)?

Show solution 
from scipy import stats

p5 = stats.poisson.pmf(5, mu=2)
print(f"P(5 in 1 min): {p5:.4f}") # 0.0361

# 5 minutes -> mu = 10
p_gt_10 = stats.poisson.sf(10, mu=10)
print(f"P(>10 in 5 min): {p_gt_10:.4f}") # 0.4170

Key terms

PDF / PMF / CDF
Density (cont) / mass (disc) / cumulative.
PPF
Inverse CDF; gives value at a percentile.
Maximum likelihood
Find params that make observed data most probable.
Q-Q plot
Visual goodness-of-fit; straight diagonal = good.

Picking the right distribution — the field guide

Your data is…DistributionExamples
Count of successes in n triesBinomial(n, p)Conversions out of 1000 visitors; heads in 20 flips
Count of events per time/space windowPoisson(λ)Support tickets/hour; defects/batch; goals/match
Continuous, symmetric, sums of many small effectsNormal(μ, σ)Measurement error; heights; averaged anything (CLT)
Waiting time between Poisson eventsExponential(λ)Time until next ticket; time between failures
Probabilities/proportions on [0,1]Beta(α, β)Conversion-rate uncertainty; Bayesian A/B testing

The scipy.stats pattern — same API for every distribution

from scipy import stats

# Every distribution has the same four methods:
dist = stats.norm(loc=100, scale=15)   # IQ-like

dist.pdf(115)        # density AT a point (relative likelihood)
dist.cdf(115)        # P(X ≤ 115) → 0.841
dist.ppf(0.95)       # inverse: value at the 95th percentile → 124.7
dist.rvs(1000)       # draw 1000 random samples

# Binomial: P(≥ 60 conversions | n=1000, p=0.05)?
1 - stats.binom(1000, 0.05).cdf(59)    # = P(X ≥ 60)

# Poisson: P(0 tickets in an hour | λ=3)?
stats.poisson(3).pmf(0)                # = e^-3 ≈ 0.0498

Memorize the quartet — pdf/pmf (density), cdf (probability below), ppf (percentile→value), rvs (samples) — and you can answer any distribution question without formulas.

The 68-95-99.7 rule and z-scores

# Normal data: 68% within ±1σ, 95% within ±2σ, 99.7% within ±3σ
z = (x - mu) / sigma          # z-score = "how many σ from the mean"

# z = 2.5 → further than 95% boundary → unusual
# |z| > 3 → outlier candidate in roughly-normal data

# Empirical check before trusting normality:
from scipy import stats
stats.probplot(data, dist="norm", plot=plt)   # Q-Q plot: straight line = normal
⚠ WHEN POISSON BREAKS

Poisson assumes variance ≈ mean. Real count data is often overdispersed (variance >> mean: viral tweets, bursty traffic). Check data.var() / data.mean() — if it's >> 1, use Negative Binomial instead. Modeling overdispersed counts as Poisson makes everything look "significant" when it isn't.

Distribution → ML connection

These aren't academic: linear regression assumes normal residuals; logistic regression models Bernoulli outcomes; Poisson regression handles counts; Beta powers Bayesian A/B tests and Thompson sampling. Recognizing which distribution your target follows tells you which model family to reach for.

# Quick distribution check workflow
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(14, 3.5))
ax[0].hist(data, bins=50)                       # shape
stats.probplot(data, dist="norm", plot=ax[1])   # vs normal
ax[2].hist(np.log1p(data), bins=50)             # does log make it normal?
# Right-skew that becomes normal after log → lognormal → model log(y)
✓ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Binomial = successes/trials; Poisson = events/window; Exponential = waits; Beta = rates
  • One API: pdf · cdf · ppf · rvs — answers any probability question
  • variance >> mean in counts → Negative Binomial, not Poisson
  • The target's distribution picks your model family (normal→OLS, binary→logistic, counts→Poisson)

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

The CLT is one of the most important results in stats: averages of samples become normal regardless of underlying distribution. This single fact powers t-tests, CIs, and most inferential statistics.

CLT in action

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Heavily skewed source
population = np.random.exponential(2, 100_000)

# Sample means converge to normal
def sample_means(pop, n, n_samples=10_000):
 return np.array([np.random.choice(pop, n).mean() for _ in range(n_samples)])

means_2 = sample_means(population, 2) # still skewed
means_30 = sample_means(population, 30) # approximately normal!
means_100 = sample_means(population, 100) # very normal

# SE = sigma / sqrt(n)
print(f"Pop std: {population.std():.3f}")
print(f"SE prediction (n=100): {population.std() / 10:.3f}")
print(f"SE actual (n=100): {means_100.std():.3f}")

Bootstrap - the Swiss army knife

import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

data = np.array([23, 25, 30, 22, 27, 26, 31, 28, 24, 29])

# Bootstrap the mean
boot_means = np.array([
 rng.choice(data, size=len(data), replace=True).mean()
 for _ in range(10_000)
])

print(f"Mean: {boot_means.mean():.2f}")
print(f"SE: {boot_means.std(ddof=1):.2f}")
print(f"95% CI: {np.percentile(boot_means, [2.5, 97.5])}")

# Works for ANY statistic - median, ratio, R^2
def bootstrap_ci(data, stat, n=10_000, alpha=0.05):
 boots = np.array([stat(rng.choice(data, len(data), replace=True))
 for _ in range(n)])
 return stat(data), np.percentile(boots, [100*alpha/2, 100*(1-alpha/2)])

med, ci = bootstrap_ci(data, np.median)

Sampling techniques

import pandas as pd
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

# Random
df.sample(n=100, random_state=42)
df.sample(frac=0.1)

# Stratified - preserve proportions
def stratified_sample(df, col, frac=0.1):
 return (df.groupby(col, group_keys=False)
 .apply(lambda g: g.sample(frac=frac, random_state=42)))

# In sklearn
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
 X, y, test_size=0.2, stratify=y, random_state=42
)

# Cluster - sample whole groups
clusters = rng.choice(df["zip"].unique(), 20, replace=False)
sample = df[df["zip"].isin(clusters)]
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

CLT requires n >= 30 as rule of thumb, but heavily skewed data needs more. With small n from non-normal data, sample means aren't normal - your t-tests and CIs are wrong. Either gather more data, transform, or use bootstrap/non-parametric methods.

Practice

Bootstrap 95% CI of the median for [12, 15, 18, 9, 22, 14, 11, 25, 19, 16] with 10K iterations.

Show solution 
import numpy as np

data = np.array([12, 15, 18, 9, 22, 14, 11, 25, 19, 16])
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

boot_medians = np.array([
 np.median(rng.choice(data, len(data), replace=True))
 for _ in range(10_000)
])

ci = np.percentile(boot_medians, [2.5, 97.5])
print(f"Median: {np.median(data)}, 95% CI: {ci}")

Key terms

Population vs sample
Whole group vs. observed subset.
Standard error
SD of a sampling distribution; SE = sigma/sqrt(n).
CLT
Sample means approximately normal for large n.
Bootstrap
Resampling with replacement; estimates sampling distribution.
Stratified sampling
Maintain proportions of subgroups in sample.

The CLT in one experiment you can run

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

# Population: WILDLY non-normal (exponential — heavily right-skewed)
population = rng.exponential(scale=10, size=1_000_000)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(16, 3))
for ax, n in zip(axes, [1, 5, 30, 200]):
    # 10,000 sample means, each from a sample of size n
    means = [rng.choice(population, n).mean() for _ in range(10_000)]
    ax.hist(means, bins=60)
    ax.set_title(f"n={n}")
# n=1: skewed like the population
# n=5: still skewed
# n=30: nearly normal  ← the classic threshold
# n=200: indistinguishable from normal

That's the Central Limit Theorem: means of samples become normal as n grows — no matter what the population looks like. This is why normal-based methods (confidence intervals, t-tests) work on means of decidedly non-normal data.

Standard error — the precision of your estimate

SE = s / np.sqrt(n)     # standard deviation OF THE SAMPLE MEAN

# n=100, s=20 → SE = 2.0
# n=400, s=20 → SE = 1.0   ← 4× the data for 2× the precision
# n=10000     → SE = 0.2   ← diminishing returns are brutal

Two facts every analyst needs: (1) SE shrinks with √n, so precision gets expensive fast — halving uncertainty costs 4× the sample. (2) σ vs SE confusion is the most common stats error in dashboards: σ describes the SPREAD OF DATA; SE describes the UNCERTAINTY OF THE MEAN.

Confidence intervals — building and reading them

from scipy import stats

sample = rng.exponential(10, size=200)
mean, se = sample.mean(), sample.std(ddof=1)/np.sqrt(len(sample))

# 95% CI (t-distribution handles small-sample uncertainty in s)
ci = stats.t.interval(0.95, df=len(sample)-1, loc=mean, scale=se)
print(f"{mean:.2f}, 95% CI [{ci[0]:.2f}, {ci[1]:.2f}]")
⚠ WHAT 95% ACTUALLY MEANS

It does NOT mean "95% probability the true mean is in this interval." It means: if we repeated this sampling procedure many times, 95% of the intervals built this way would contain the true mean. The procedure has a 95% capture rate; any single interval either contains it or doesn't. Subtle, but interviewers love it.

Bootstrap — when formulas don't exist

# SE of the MEDIAN? Of a ratio? No clean formula — bootstrap it.
def bootstrap_ci(data, stat_fn, n_boot=10_000, ci=95):
    boots = [stat_fn(rng.choice(data, len(data), replace=True))
             for _ in range(n_boot)]
    lo, hi = np.percentile(boots, [(100-ci)/2, 100-(100-ci)/2])
    return lo, hi

bootstrap_ci(sample, np.median)        # CI for the median
bootstrap_ci(sample, lambda x: x.std())  # CI for the std — works for ANY statistic

Resample your own data with replacement, recompute the statistic thousands of times, take percentiles. It works for medians, ratios, AUCs, anything — the universal tool when theory runs out.

How big a sample do I need?

# Detect a difference d with std s at 95% confidence, 80% power:
# n ≈ 16 * (s/d)²        (the classic rule of thumb per group)

s, d = 20, 5
n = 16 * (s/d)**2        # = 256 per group
# Halve the detectable difference → 4× the sample. Plan accordingly.
✓ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • CLT: sample means go normal (~n≥30) regardless of population shape
  • SE = s/√n — precision costs quadratically; σ ≠ SE
  • 95% CI describes the PROCEDURE's capture rate, not one interval's probability
  • Bootstrap gives CIs for any statistic when formulas don't exist

Exercise form: histogram the simulated means — plt.hist(means, bins=30) — watching that histogram go bell-shaped IS the central limit theorem.

📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Point estimates lie. CIs say how confident to be. They're the bridge between sample stats and population claims, the foundation of inference.

CI for a mean

import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

sample = np.array([72, 68, 75, 80, 65, 70, 78, 82, 74, 76])
n = len(sample)
mean = sample.mean()
sem = stats.sem(sample)

# t-CI (use when sigma unknown - almost always)
ci = stats.t.interval(0.95, df=n-1, loc=mean, scale=sem)
print(f"Mean: {mean:.2f}, 95% CI: {ci}")

# Bootstrap CI - no distributional assumptions
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
boots = np.array([rng.choice(sample, n, replace=True).mean()
 for _ in range(10_000)])
ci_boot = np.percentile(boots, [2.5, 97.5])

CI for a proportion

# 60 heads in 100 flips
from statsmodels.stats.proportion import proportion_confint

# Wald - simple, can be wrong near 0 or 1
ci_wald = proportion_confint(60, 100, method="normal")

# Wilson - much better near boundaries - PREFERRED
ci_wilson = proportion_confint(60, 100, method="wilson")

# Clopper-Pearson - exact (conservative)
ci_exact = proportion_confint(60, 100, method="beta")

# For small p (e.g., 5/100), Wald and Wilson differ noticeably
# Always use Wilson by default

CI for difference of means

group_a = np.array([78, 82, 85, 80, 79, 88, 81])
group_b = np.array([72, 75, 70, 78, 71, 74, 76])

# Welch's t-test (unequal variances) - safer default
from scipy.stats import ttest_ind
t, p = ttest_ind(group_a, group_b, equal_var=False)

# Use pingouin for cleaner output (effect size, CI included)
# import pingouin as pg
# pg.ttest(group_a, group_b, correction=True)

# Manual CI for the difference
diff = group_a.mean() - group_b.mean()
se = np.sqrt(group_a.var(ddof=1)/len(group_a) +
 group_b.var(ddof=1)/len(group_b))
# Welch-Satterthwaite df is computed automatically in test
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

A 95% CI does NOT mean "95% probability the parameter is in here". It's a statement about the procedure: across many repeats, 95% of such intervals would contain the true value. The Bayesian credible interval IS a probability statement, but requires a prior.

Common CI mistakes

  • Confusing CI with prediction interval (PI is wider - includes residual variability).
  • Comparing CIs visually instead of running a proper test (overlapping CIs do NOT imply p > 0.05).
  • Not adjusting for multiple comparisons (testing 100 things at α=0.05 -> ~5 false positives).
  • Reporting only point estimate without CI.

Practice

23 clicks out of 200 visitors. Compute Wald and Wilson 95% CIs. Why is Wilson preferred?

Show solution 
from statsmodels.stats.proportion import proportion_confint

ci_wald = proportion_confint(23, 200, method="normal")
ci_wilson = proportion_confint(23, 200, method="wilson")

print(f"Wald: {ci_wald}") # ~ (0.071, 0.159)
print(f"Wilson: {ci_wilson}") # ~ (0.077, 0.166)

# Wald assumes normal approx that breaks down for small p (p̂=0.115).
# Wilson is asymmetric and stays valid - use as default.

Key terms

Confidence interval
Range capturing parameter in (1-α) of repeated samples.
Standard error
SD of sampling distribution.
Wald vs Wilson CI
Methods for proportion CI; Wilson preferred.
Bootstrap CI
Resampling-based; no distributional assumptions.
Prediction interval
Where next observation likely; wider than CI.

📖 DEFINITIONS AT A GLANCE — key terms in this section
TermDefinition
Null (H₀)default - no effect.
Alt (Hₐ)what you want to detect.
p-valueP(test stat this extreme | H₀ true).
Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.
📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Hypothesis tests answer 'is the difference real or chance?'. They're the language of A/B tests, papers, and decisions. Knowing when to use which test - and what p-values mean - prevents most stats misuse.

The framework

  • Null (H₀): default - no effect.
  • Alt (Hₐ): what you want to detect.
  • p-value: P(test stat this extreme | H₀ true). NOT P(H₀ true).
  • α: pre-chosen threshold. Reject H₀ if p ≤ α.
  • Type I false positive (rate α). Type II false negative (rate β). Power = 1-β.

t-test variants

from scipy import stats

# Two independent groups - Welch's (unequal var)
t, p = stats.ttest_ind(control, treatment, equal_var=False)

# One-sample - vs known value
t, p = stats.ttest_1samp(sample, popmean=80)

# Paired - same subjects measured twice
t, p = stats.ttest_rel(before, after)

# One-tailed
t, p_two = stats.ttest_ind(treatment, control, equal_var=False)
p_one = p_two / 2 if t > 0 else 1 - p_two/2

# Effect size (Cohen's d) - more useful than p alone
def cohens_d(a, b):
 pooled = np.sqrt((a.var(ddof=1) + b.var(ddof=1)) / 2)
 return (a.mean() - b.mean()) / pooled
# d=0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large

Non-parametric and categorical

# Non-parametric (no normality assumption)
stats.mannwhitneyu(a, b, alternative="two-sided") # vs t-test
stats.wilcoxon(before, after) # vs paired
stats.kruskal(g1, g2, g3) # vs ANOVA

# Categorical
import numpy as np
ctab = np.array(5095070930)
chi2, p, dof, expected = stats.chi2_contingency(ctab)

# Small counts (<5) -> Fisher exact
stats.fisher_exact(8219)

# Two-proportion z-test (cleanest for A/B)
from statsmodels.stats.proportion import proportions_ztest
z, p = proportions_ztest([50, 70], [1000, 1000])

# 3+ groups
f, p = stats.f_oneway(g1, g2, g3) # one-way ANOVA
# Post-hoc Tukey
from statsmodels.stats.multicomp import pairwise_tukeyhsd
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Multiple comparisons inflate Type I error. Test 100 hypotheses at α=0.05 -> expect 5 false positives just by chance. Use Bonferroni (α/n) or False Discovery Rate corrections. Pre-register hypotheses to avoid p-hacking.

Power analysis

from statsmodels.stats.power import TTestIndPower
import numpy as np

analysis = TTestIndPower()

# n needed for d=0.5, alpha=0.05, power=0.80
n = analysis.solve_power(effect_size=0.5, alpha=0.05, power=0.80)
print(f"Need n = {np.ceil(n):.0f}")

# What effect can n=50 detect?
detectable = analysis.solve_power(nobs1=50, alpha=0.05, power=0.80)

# For proportions
from statsmodels.stats.power import NormalIndPower
from statsmodels.stats.proportion import proportion_effectsize

# Detect 6% vs 5% baseline
es = proportion_effectsize(0.06, 0.05)
n_per_arm = NormalIndPower().solve_power(es, alpha=0.05, power=0.80)

p-value: what it actually means

  • P(test stat this extreme | H₀ true). Just one piece of evidence.
  • It is NOT the probability H₀ is true.
  • Always report effect size, CI, sample size alongside p.
  • With huge n, tiny effects become significant - check magnitude.

Practice

Control 50/1000, treatment 70/1000. (a) Test difference. (b) Lift and CI. (c) Power for 20% relative lift on 5% baseline?

Show solution 
from statsmodels.stats.proportion import proportions_ztest, proportion_effectsize
from statsmodels.stats.power import NormalIndPower
import numpy as np

# (a)
z, p = proportions_ztest([50, 70], [1000, 1000])
print(f"z = {z:.3f}, p = {p:.4f}")

# (b)
p_a, p_b = 50/1000, 70/1000
lift = (p_b - p_a) / p_a
diff = p_b - p_a
se = np.sqrt(p_a*(1-p_a)/1000 + p_b*(1-p_b)/1000)
ci = (diff - 1.96*se, diff + 1.96*se)
print(f"Lift: {lift:.1%}, CI: {ci}")

# (c) Power
es = proportion_effectsize(0.06, 0.05)
power = NormalIndPower().solve_power(es, alpha=0.05, nobs1=1000)
print(f"Power: {power:.2f}") # underpowered

Key terms

Null hypothesis
Default of no effect.
p-value
P(stat this extreme | H₀ true).
Type I/II error
False positive / false negative.
Power
1-β; ability to detect a real effect.
Effect size
Magnitude (Cohen's d, lift); independent of n.
Multiple comparisons
Adjust α when testing many hypotheses.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

A/B tests drive product decisions at every modern tech company. Knowing how to size, monitor, analyze, and avoid pitfalls is one of the highest-leverage data-science skills.

Sample size determination

from statsmodels.stats.power import NormalIndPower
from statsmodels.stats.proportion import proportion_effectsize
import numpy as np

# Decide BEFORE running:
# 1. Baseline (5% conversion)
# 2. MDE (smallest meaningful lift, e.g., +20% relative -> 6%)
# 3. alpha (0.05), power (0.80)

baseline = 0.05
mde_relative = 0.20
target = baseline * (1 + mde_relative)

es = proportion_effectsize(target, baseline)
n_per_arm = NormalIndPower().solve_power(es, alpha=0.05, power=0.80)
print(f"Need {np.ceil(n_per_arm):.0f} per arm")

# For continuous metrics
from statsmodels.stats.power import TTestIndPower
n = TTestIndPower().solve_power(effect_size=0.10, alpha=0.05, power=0.80)

Hash-based assignment

import hashlib

def assign_variant(user_id, exp_id, variants):
 """Deterministic, replayable randomization."""
 h = hashlib.md5(f"{exp_id}:{user_id}".encode()).hexdigest()
 return variants[int(h, 16) % len(variants)]

# Same user always gets same variant
assign_variant("alice", "exp_2024", ["control", "treatment"])

# Stratified - balance covariates
# Cluster - assign whole groups (schools, marketplaces)
# Switchback - alternate variants over time

Analyzing results

import pandas as pd
from statsmodels.stats.proportion import proportions_ztest
import numpy as np

results = pd.DataFrame({
 "variant": ["control", "treatment"],
 "users": [10000, 10000],
 "conversions": [510, 580],
})

z, p = proportions_ztest(
 results["conversions"], results["users"]
)

# Bootstrap CI for difference
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
def bootstrap_diff(c_conv, c_n, t_conv, t_n, n_boots=10_000):
 c = np.array([1]*c_conv + [0]*(c_n-c_conv))
 t = np.array([1]*t_conv + [0]*(t_n-t_conv))
 diffs = np.array([
 rng.choice(t, len(t), replace=True).mean() -
 rng.choice(c, len(c), replace=True).mean()
 for _ in range(n_boots)
 ])
 return np.percentile(diffs, [2.5, 97.5])

ci = bootstrap_diff(510, 10000, 580, 10000)
lift = (580/10000 - 510/10000) / (510/10000)
print(f"Lift: {lift:.1%}, CI: {ci}")

Common pitfalls

  • Peeking: looking before sample size reached. Inflates Type I error from 5% to ~30%+. Pre-commit or use sequential testing.
  • Multiple metrics: 10 metrics at α=0.05 = 40% false-positive rate. Adjust or pre-register primary.
  • Novelty effect: new things look better in week 1, fade after. Run for full business cycle.
  • Network effects: treatment users influence control. Use cluster randomization.
  • Statistical vs practical significance: huge n makes tiny effects 'significant'. Check effect size matters for decisions.
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Stopping early at first p<0.05 is the most common A/B mistake. "It's already significant after 2 days" is exactly what you'd see by chance with peeking. Either pre-commit to sample size or use Bayesian/sequential methods.

Bayesian A/B (no peeking penalty)

import numpy as np

class BayesianAB:
 def __init__(self):
 self.alpha = [1, 1] # successes for A, B
 self.beta = [1, 1] # failures
 def update(self, variant, succ, fail):
 self.alpha[variant] += succ
 self.beta[variant] += fail
 def prob_b_better(self, n=10_000):
 rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
 a = rng.beta(self.alpha[0], self.beta[0], n)
 b = rng.beta(self.alpha[1], self.beta[1], n)
 return (b > a).mean()

ab = BayesianAB()
ab.update(0, 510, 9490)
ab.update(1, 580, 9420)
print(f"P(treatment better): {ab.prob_b_better():.3f}")
# Update as data arrives - no peeking penalty in Bayesian framework

Practice

Plan a test: baseline conversion 3%, MDE = +0.5pp absolute, α=0.05, power=0.8. How many users per arm?

Show solution 
from statsmodels.stats.power import NormalIndPower
from statsmodels.stats.proportion import proportion_effectsize
import numpy as np

es = proportion_effectsize(0.035, 0.03)
n = NormalIndPower().solve_power(es, alpha=0.05, power=0.80)
print(f"Need {np.ceil(n):.0f} per arm = {np.ceil(2*n):.0f} total")
# ~ 12,000 per arm = 24,000 total

Key terms

MDE
Minimum detectable effect; smallest lift you care about.
Power
P(detect real effect); typically 80%.
Peeking
Checking results before sample reached - inflates Type I.
Sequential testing
Methods that allow safe peeking.
Guardrail metrics
Secondary metrics that mustn't regress.

Formula: the pooled proportion for a two-proportion test — p_pool = (x1 + x2) / (n1 + n2) — combined successes over combined sample sizes, used in the standard error under H0.

Most production data lives in databases, not CSVs. SQLAlchemy is the standard way Python talks to SQL — works with PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, Snowflake, BigQuery. Pandas integrates seamlessly via read_sql.

Connecting and reading

# pip install sqlalchemy psycopg2-binary
import sqlalchemy as sa
import pandas as pd

# Connection strings (DSN)
# postgresql://user:pass@host:5432/dbname
# mysql+pymysql://user:pass@host/dbname
# sqlite:///path/to/file.db
# snowflake://user:pass@account/db/schema?warehouse=...

engine = sa.create_engine("sqlite:///mydb.db")

# Read into DataFrame
df = pd.read_sql("SELECT * FROM customers WHERE country = 'US'", engine)

# Parameterized - PREVENTS SQL INJECTION
df = pd.read_sql(
 "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE country = :c",
 engine,
 params={"c": "US"}
)

# Read with chunking - for big tables
for chunk in pd.read_sql("SELECT * FROM huge_table", engine, chunksize=100_000):
 process(chunk)

Writing data back

# Append a DataFrame as a table
df.to_sql("results", engine, if_exists="append", index=False)

# Replace whole table
df.to_sql("results", engine, if_exists="replace", index=False)

# Fail if exists (default - prevents accidents)
df.to_sql("results", engine, if_exists="fail", index=False)

# Specify column types
import sqlalchemy.types as t
df.to_sql("results", engine, if_exists="replace", index=False,
 dtype={"id": t.Integer, "name": t.String(100)})

# Bulk insert with chunksize - much faster
df.to_sql("big_table", engine, if_exists="append", index=False,
 chunksize=10_000, method="multi")

Connection management

# Always use context managers
with engine.connect() as conn:
 result = conn.execute(sa.text("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders"))
 count = result.scalar()
 print(f"Orders: {count}")

# Multiple statements with transaction
with engine.begin() as conn:
 conn.execute(sa.text("UPDATE orders SET status='archived' WHERE date < :d"),
 {"d": "2020-01-01"})
 conn.execute(sa.text("INSERT INTO archive SELECT * FROM orders WHERE date < :d"),
 {"d": "2020-01-01"})
 # Auto-commits on success, rolls back on exception

# Connection pooling - for web apps
engine = sa.create_engine(
 "postgresql://...",
 pool_size=10,
 max_overflow=20,
 pool_pre_ping=True, # check connection before using
 pool_recycle=3600,
)
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

NEVER concatenate user input into SQL strings. f"WHERE name = '{name}'" is a SQL injection bug. Always use parameterized queries (:name) or SQLAlchemy's expression language.

Reading directly to/from S3 / cloud

# Modern alternative: DuckDB - SQL on parquet/csv with no DB server
# pip install duckdb
import duckdb

# Query a parquet file directly
df = duckdb.query("""
 SELECT category, AVG(price) as avg_price, COUNT(*) as n
 FROM 'data/products.parquet'
 GROUP BY category
""").to_df()

# Join across files
df = duckdb.query("""
 SELECT o.*, c.country
 FROM 'orders.parquet' o
 JOIN 'customers.parquet' c ON o.customer_id = c.id
 WHERE o.amount > 100
""").to_df()

# Read from S3 (with pyarrow + s3fs)
df = pd.read_parquet("s3://my-bucket/data.parquet")

# CSV from URL
df = pd.read_csv("https://example.com/data.csv")

Practice

Connect to a SQLite database, read all orders into a DataFrame using parameterized query (year=2024), aggregate by month, and save the summary back as a new table.

Show solution 
import sqlalchemy as sa
import pandas as pd

engine = sa.create_engine("sqlite:///orders.db")

df = pd.read_sql(
 "SELECT * FROM orders WHERE strftime('%Y', date) = :year",
 engine,
 params={"year": "2024"},
 parse_dates=["date"],
)

monthly = (
 df.assign(month=df["date"].dt.to_period("M"))
 .groupby("month", as_index=False)
 .agg(orders=("id", "count"), revenue=("amount", "sum"))
)
monthly["month"] = monthly["month"].astype(str)

monthly.to_sql("monthly_summary_2024", engine, if_exists="replace", index=False)
print(f"Saved {len(monthly)} rows")

Key terms

SQLAlchemy engine
Connection pool object - reuse, don't recreate.
Parameterized query
Safe input substitution; prevents SQL injection.
read_sql / to_sql
Pandas methods for DB I/O.
Connection pool
Reusable connections; saves auth/setup overhead.
DuckDB
In-process SQL on files; great for analytics.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Production databases have things test files don't: huge tables, slow queries, joins across tables, type oddities. Knowing how to query efficiently and handle real-world quirks is what makes you useful on day one.

Efficient query patterns

import pandas as pd
import sqlalchemy as sa

engine = sa.create_engine("postgresql://...")

# 1. Filter at DB, not in pandas
# BAD: pull whole table, then filter
df = pd.read_sql("SELECT * FROM events", engine)
df_recent = df[df["date"] > "2024-01-01"] # wastes memory + time

# GOOD: filter at source
df_recent = pd.read_sql(
 "SELECT * FROM events WHERE date > '2024-01-01'", engine
)

# 2. Select only needed columns
df = pd.read_sql("SELECT id, customer_id, amount FROM orders", engine)
# Don't SELECT *

# 3. Aggregate at DB when possible
summary = pd.read_sql("""
 SELECT region, COUNT(*) as n, SUM(amount) as total
 FROM orders
 WHERE date >= '2024-01-01'
 GROUP BY region
""", engine)
# Saves transferring millions of rows just to GROUP BY

# 4. Use indexes - check EXPLAIN
result = pd.read_sql("EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 123", engine)

Joins across tables

# Strategy A: join in SQL (best for big tables)
df = pd.read_sql("""
 SELECT o.id, o.amount, c.name, c.country, p.category
 FROM orders o
 LEFT JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id
 LEFT JOIN products p ON o.product_id = p.id
 WHERE o.date >= '2024-01-01'
""", engine)

# Strategy B: pull tables, merge in pandas (good for small tables, faster iteration)
orders = pd.read_sql("SELECT * FROM orders WHERE date >= '2024-01-01'", engine)
customers = pd.read_sql("SELECT id, name, country FROM customers", engine)
products = pd.read_sql("SELECT id, category FROM products", engine)

merged = (orders
 .merge(customers, left_on="customer_id", right_on="id", suffixes=("", "_c"))
 .merge(products, left_on="product_id", right_on="id", suffixes=("", "_p")))

# Choose A when joining big tables (DB optimizes the join)
# Choose B when iterating analysis or small tables fit in RAM

Type handling and dates

# Force dates parsed correctly
df = pd.read_sql("SELECT * FROM events", engine,
 parse_dates=["created_at", "updated_at"])

# Custom date format
df = pd.read_sql("SELECT * FROM events", engine,
 parse_dates={"date_str": {"format": "%Y%m%d"}})

# Force types
import numpy as np
df = pd.read_sql("SELECT * FROM products", engine,
 dtype={"id": str, "price": np.float32})

# DECIMAL columns come in as Python Decimal - convert to float
df["price"] = df["price"].astype(float)

# Postgres JSON columns - already parsed if reading via SQLAlchemy
# MySQL: store as text, parse manually
import json
df["meta_dict"] = df["meta_json"].apply(json.loads)

Time-bounded incremental loads

# For "load new records since last run" patterns
from datetime import datetime, timedelta

last_run = datetime.now() - timedelta(days=1)

new_data = pd.read_sql(
 "SELECT * FROM events WHERE created_at > :ts",
 engine,
 params={"ts": last_run},
 parse_dates=["created_at"],
)

# Save state for next run
import json
from pathlib import Path

state = {"last_run": datetime.now().isoformat()}
Path("state.json").write_text(json.dumps(state))

# Read state at start of next run
state = json.loads(Path("state.json").read_text())
last_run = datetime.fromisoformat(state["last_run"])
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Long-running queries can hold transactions open and lock tables. Set query timeouts: engine.execute('SET statement_timeout=30000') in Postgres. Use read replicas for analytics, not the primary OLTP database. Add LIMIT during exploration; never run unbounded queries on prod.

Pagination for huge results

# Reading 50M rows? Don't pull all at once.

# Pattern 1: chunksize
for chunk in pd.read_sql("SELECT * FROM big_table", engine, chunksize=100_000):
 summary = chunk.groupby("category").size()
 save_partial(summary)

# Pattern 2: explicit OFFSET pagination (slow at high offsets)
page = 0
size = 10_000
while True:
 df = pd.read_sql(
 f"SELECT * FROM events ORDER BY id LIMIT {size} OFFSET {page * size}",
 engine
 )
 if df.empty:
 break
 process(df)
 page += 1

# Pattern 3: keyset pagination (fast)
last_id = 0
while True:
 df = pd.read_sql(
 "SELECT * FROM events WHERE id > :id ORDER BY id LIMIT 10000",
 engine,
 params={"id": last_id},
 )
 if df.empty:
 break
 process(df)
 last_id = df["id"].max()

Practice

Pull all customers in 'US' with their order count and total spend in 2024 in a single SQL query. Then in pandas, get the top 10 customers by spend.

Show solution 
import pandas as pd
import sqlalchemy as sa

engine = sa.create_engine("postgresql://...")

df = pd.read_sql("""
 SELECT c.id, c.name, c.email,
 COUNT(o.id) as n_orders,
 COALESCE(SUM(o.amount), 0) as total_spend
 FROM customers c
 LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
 AND o.date >= '2024-01-01'
 AND o.date < '2025-01-01'
 WHERE c.country = 'US'
 GROUP BY c.id, c.name, c.email
""", engine)

top10 = df.nlargest(10, "total_spend")
print(top10)

Key terms

Push-down
Doing filtering/aggregation at the DB instead of in pandas.
OLTP vs OLAP
Operational vs analytics workloads; analytics belongs on replicas.
Keyset pagination
WHERE id > last_id; faster than OFFSET on big tables.
chunksize
pd.read_sql parameter that returns iterator of chunks.
Read replica
Read-only DB copy used for analytics to spare the primary.

Exercise calls: write a DataFrame to SQL replacing the table — df.to_sql("sales", engine, if_exists="replace", index=False) — or add rows to what exists with if_exists="append". replace drops and recreates; append inserts — appending adds new rows beneath the existing ones.

APIs are the modern way to get data: stock prices, weather, social media, internal microservices. The requests library is the de-facto Python standard for HTTP — clean, batteries-included, the right level of abstraction.

Basic requests

# pip install requests
import requests

# GET
r = requests.get("https://api.github.com/repos/python/cpython")
print(r.status_code) # 200
print(r.json()) # parsed JSON

# Query parameters
r = requests.get(
 "https://api.github.com/search/repositories",
 params={"q": "language:python stars:>10000", "per_page": 5},
)

# POST with JSON body
r = requests.post(
 "https://api.example.com/events",
 json={"event": "click", "user_id": 42},
)

# POST form data
r = requests.post(
 "https://api.example.com/login",
 data={"username": "alice", "password": "secret"},
)

# Headers (auth, content-type, etc.)
r = requests.get(
 "https://api.example.com/data",
 headers={
 "Authorization": "Bearer YOUR_TOKEN",
 "User-Agent": "MyApp/1.0",
 "Accept": "application/json",
 },
)

Response inspection

r = requests.get("https://api.github.com/repos/python/cpython")

r.status_code # 200
r.ok # True if 200-299
r.url # final URL after redirects
r.headers # response headers (dict-like)
r.cookies # cookie jar
r.text # body as string
r.content # body as bytes (binary)
r.json() # parsed JSON

# Error handling
try:
 r.raise_for_status() # raises HTTPError for 4xx/5xx
except requests.HTTPError as e:
 print(f"Failed: {e}")

# Stream large responses
with requests.get(url, stream=True) as r:
 with open("big_file.zip", "wb") as f:
 for chunk in r.iter_content(chunk_size=8192):
 f.write(chunk)

Sessions for performance

# Session reuses connections (faster + cleaner)
import requests

session = requests.Session()
session.headers.update({
 "User-Agent": "MyApp/1.0",
 "Authorization": "Bearer TOKEN",
})

# Now every request uses the session's headers
r1 = session.get("https://api.example.com/users/1")
r2 = session.get("https://api.example.com/users/2")
# 2nd request reuses TCP+TLS connection - much faster

# Mounting adapters with retry logic
from requests.adapters import HTTPAdapter
from urllib3.util.retry import Retry

retry = Retry(
 total=5,
 backoff_factor=0.5, # 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8 seconds between retries
 status_forcelist=[429, 500, 502, 503, 504],
 allowed_methods=["GET", "POST"],
)
session.mount("https://", HTTPAdapter(max_retries=retry))

JSON to DataFrame

import requests
import pandas as pd

Always set timeouts. requests.get(url) with no timeout will hang forever if the server doesn't respond. Default to timeout=10 or use a tuple (connect_timeout, read_timeout). In production: set retries, log failures, alert on persistent errors.

Error handling pattern

import requests
import time

def fetch_with_retry(url, max_retries=3, **kwargs):
 """Fetch with exponential backoff and proper error handling."""
 kwargs.setdefault("timeout", 10)

 for attempt in range(max_retries):
 try:
 r = requests.get(url, **kwargs)
 r.raise_for_status()
 return r.json()
 except requests.HTTPError as e:
 if r.status_code == 429: # rate limited
 wait = int(r.headers.get("Retry-After", 60))
 print(f"Rate limited, waiting {wait}s...")
 time.sleep(wait)
 elif r.status_code >= 500: # server error
 if attempt == max_retries - 1: raise
 time.sleep(2 ** attempt)
 else:
 raise # don't retry 4xx (except 429)
 except requests.Timeout:
 if attempt == max_retries - 1: raise
 time.sleep(2 ** attempt)
 except requests.ConnectionError:
 if attempt == max_retries - 1: raise
 time.sleep(2 ** attempt)
 return None

APIs return structured data — usually JSON, sometimes XML. Knowing how to navigate nested structures, flatten them into rows, and handle missing fields is essential for any data-from-API workflow.

JSON basics

import json

# Parse JSON string
text = '{"name": "Alice", "age": 30, "tags": ["a", "b"]}'
data = json.loads(text)
print(data["name"]) # "Alice"

# Pretty-print
print(json.dumps(data, indent=2, sort_keys=True))

# From file
with open("data.json") as f:
 data = json.load(f)

# To file
with open("output.json", "w") as f:
 json.dump(data, f, indent=2)

# Date handling - json.dump can't serialize datetime
from datetime import datetime
data = {"timestamp": datetime.now()}

# Bad: TypeError
# json.dumps(data)

# Good: convert first or use default=
json.dumps(data, default=str)
json.dumps({"timestamp": datetime.now().isoformat()})

Nested JSON to DataFrame

import pandas as pd

response = [
 {
 "id": 1,
 "user": {"name": "Alice", "address": {"city": "NYC", "zip": "10001"}},
 "orders": [
 {"item": "book", "price": 15},
 {"item": "pen", "price": 2},
 ],
 },
 {
 "id": 2,
 "user": {"name": "Bob", "address": {"city": "SF", "zip": "94101"}},
 "orders": [{"item": "lamp", "price": 50}],
 },
]

# Flatten - one row per top-level item
users = pd.json_normalize(response, sep="_")
# Columns: id, user_name, user_address_city, user_address_zip, orders

# Flatten - one row per nested item
orders = pd.json_normalize(
 response,
 record_path="orders", # the array to expand
 meta=["id", ["user", "name"]], # parent fields to include
 meta_prefix="parent_",
)
# Columns: item, price, parent_id, parent_user.name

Defensive parsing

# API responses often have missing fields - handle gracefully

def safe_get(d, path, default=None):
 """Walk a nested dict by path."""
 for key in path:
 if not isinstance(d, dict): return default
 if key not in d: return default
 d = d[key]
 return d

# Use it
city = safe_get(response[0], ["user", "address", "city"], "Unknown")

# Or with .get() chain
city = (response[0]
 .get("user", {})
 .get("address", {})
 .get("city", "Unknown"))

When parsing JSON from APIs you don't control, ALWAYS validate. Schema can change without notice; missing fields can crash production. Use defensive defaults or schema validation (pydantic, jsonschema). Log unexpected payloads so you find drifts early.

Working with paginated APIs

import requests
import pandas as pd

def fetch_all_pages(url, params=None, max_pages=100):
 """Generic paginated fetcher (offset-style)."""
 all_results = []
 params = params or {}
 page = 1

 while page <= max_pages:
 params["page"] = page
 params["per_page"] = 100
 r = requests.get(url, params=params, timeout=10)
 r.raise_for_status()
 data = r.json()

 if not data: # empty page = done
 break

 all_results.extend(data)
 page += 1

 return all_results

# Some APIs use cursor pagination
def fetch_cursor(url, params=None):
 all_results = []
 params = params or {}
 while True:
 r = requests.get(url, params=params, timeout=10)
 r.raise_for_status()
 data = r.json()
 all_results.extend(data["results"])
 if not data.get("next_cursor"):
 break
 params["cursor"] = data["next_cursor"]
 return all_results

Every real API requires auth (API key, OAuth, JWT) and enforces rate limits. Knowing how to authenticate, store secrets safely, and respect quotas is what separates working scripts from breaking ones.

API key auth

import os
import requests

# Load key from env (NEVER hardcode)
api_key = os.environ["OPENAI_API_KEY"]

# Header-based (most common)
r = requests.get(
 "https://api.example.com/data",
 headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}"},
)

# Query param (less common, less secure - logged in URLs)
r = requests.get(
 "https://api.example.com/data",
 params={"api_key": api_key},
)

# Custom header
r = requests.get(
 "https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/weather",
 headers={"X-API-Key": api_key},
)

# Loading .env files
# pip install python-dotenv
from dotenv import load_dotenv
load_dotenv() # loads .env into os.environ
api_key = os.environ["MY_API_KEY"]

OAuth and JWT

# OAuth 2.0 - common for user-data APIs (Google, GitHub, Slack)
# Flow: app gets authorization code -> exchanges for access token

import requests

# Step 1: redirect user to authorize URL (manual in scripts; lib in apps)
# https://accounts.google.com/o/oauth2/auth?client_id=...&redirect_uri=...&scope=...

# Step 2: exchange code for token
r = requests.post(
 "https://oauth2.googleapis.com/token",
 data={
 "code": auth_code,
 "client_id": client_id,
 "client_secret": client_secret,
 "redirect_uri": redirect_uri,
 "grant_type": "authorization_code",
 },
)
tokens = r.json()
access_token = tokens["access_token"]
refresh_token = tokens["refresh_token"]

# Step 3: use access token
r = requests.get(
 "https://www.googleapis.com/oauth2/v2/userinfo",
 headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {access_token}"},
)

# Refresh when expired
r = requests.post(
 "https://oauth2.googleapis.com/token",
 data={
 "refresh_token": refresh_token,
 "client_id": client_id,
 "client_secret": client_secret,
 "grant_type": "refresh_token",
 },
)

# Libraries that handle this for you:
# - requests-oauthlib
# - authlib
# - Auth0/Okta SDKs

Rate limiting and pagination together

import requests
import time

class RateLimitedClient:
 def __init__(self, base_url, api_key, calls_per_minute=60):
 self.base_url = base_url
 self.session = requests.Session()
 self.session.headers["Authorization"] = f"Bearer {api_key}"
 self.min_interval = 60 / calls_per_minute
 self.last_call = 0

 def _wait(self):
 elapsed = time.time() - self.last_call
 if elapsed < self.min_interval:
 time.sleep(self.min_interval - elapsed)

 def get(self, path, **kwargs):
 self._wait()
 kwargs.setdefault("timeout", 10)
 for attempt in range(5):
 r = self.session.get(f"{self.base_url}{path}", **kwargs)
 self.last_call = time.time()

 if r.status_code == 429: # rate limited
 wait = int(r.headers.get("Retry-After", 2 ** attempt))
 print(f"429 - waiting {wait}s")
 time.sleep(wait)
 continue
 if 500 <= r.status_code < 600: # server error
 time.sleep(2 ** attempt)
 continue
 r.raise_for_status()
 return r.json()
 raise RuntimeError("Max retries exceeded")

client = RateLimitedClient("https://api.example.com", api_key)
data = client.get("/users/me")
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Never commit API keys. Use a pre-commit hook (e.g., detect-secrets, truffleHog) to catch them before they hit GitHub. If you accidentally commit one, ROTATE IT immediately - removing the commit doesn't help; it's already in clones, forks, and forever in GitHub's archive.

Webhooks and event-driven APIs

# Webhooks: server pushes events to your endpoint
# Common for: Slack, GitHub, Stripe, Twilio

# 1. Set up an endpoint to receive POST requests
# Using FastAPI as example:

from fastapi import FastAPI, Request, HTTPException
import hmac
import hashlib

app = FastAPI()

WEBHOOK_SECRET = os.environ["WEBHOOK_SECRET"]

@app.post("/webhook/stripe")
async def stripe_webhook(request: Request):
 payload = await request.body()
 sig_header = request.headers.get("stripe-signature", "")

 # Verify signature - prevents impersonation
 expected = hmac.new(
 WEBHOOK_SECRET.encode(),
 payload,
 hashlib.sha256
 ).hexdigest()

 if not hmac.compare_digest(expected, sig_header):
 raise HTTPException(401, "Invalid signature")

 event = await request.json()
 if event["type"] == "charge.succeeded":
 record_payment(event["data"]["object"])

 return {"received": True}

# Always: verify signature, return 2xx quickly, do work async,
# handle duplicates (events can arrive twice)

import os, time, requests

API_KEY = os.environ["API_KEY"]
session = requests.Session()
session.headers["Authorization"] = f"Bearer {API_KEY}"
INTERVAL = 60 / 60 # 1 second between calls

def fetch_all(url, params=None):
 results = []

 while True:
 params["page"] = page
 time.sleep(INTERVAL)

 r = session.get(url, params=params, timeout=10)

API key
Static secret string for auth; simplest method.
OAuth 2.0
Token-based auth with user delegation; refresh tokens.
JWT
JSON Web Token; signed claims; common for APIs.
Rate limit
API constraint: e.g., 60/min; 429 status when exceeded.
Webhook
Server-to-server push notification; always verify signatures.
Backoff
Wait progressively longer between retries.
