Free-text output is fine for chat, terrible for pipelines. Structured outputs (JSON, validated against schemas) let LLMs feed into the rest of your code reliably. This is the bridge between probabilistic LLMs and deterministic systems.

JSON output with prefill

from anthropic import Anthropic
import json
client = Anthropic()

# Trick: prefill the assistant turn to start with "{". Forces JSON.
def extract_json(text: str, max_tokens: int = 500) -> dict:
 r = client.messages.create(
 model="claude-haiku-4-5-20251001",
 max_tokens=max_tokens, temperature=0,
 messages=[
 {"role": "user", "content": text},
 {"role": "assistant", "content": "{"}, # prefill
 ],
 stop_sequences=["}"], # we'll add the closing brace
 )
 raw = "{" + r.content[0].text + "}"
 return json.loads(raw)

# Use case: structured extraction
extracted = extract_json("""
Extract: name, email, phone from this text. JSON keys: name, email, phone.

"Hi, this is Alice Wonderland (alice@example.com or 555-1234)."
""")

Pydantic-validated outputs

# Pydantic gives you schema validation + type safety
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, ValidationError, EmailStr
from typing import Optional, Literal

class Contact(BaseModel):
 name: str
 email: Optional[EmailStr] = None
 phone: Optional[str] = None
 role: Literal["customer", "lead", "vendor", "unknown"] = "unknown"

def extract_contact(text: str, max_retries: int = 2) -> Contact:
 """Extract contact info, retry on validation failure."""
 schema_str = json.dumps(Contact.model_json_schema(), indent=2)

 prompt = f"""Extract contact information from the text. Return JSON conforming exactly to this schema:

{schema_str}

Text: """
{text}
"""

Output JSON:"""

 for attempt in range(max_retries):
 r = client.messages.create(
 model="claude-haiku-4-5-20251001", max_tokens=500, temperature=0,
 messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt},
 {"role": "assistant", "content": "{"}],
 stop_sequences=["}"],
 )
 raw = "{" + r.content[0].text + "}"
 try:
 return Contact.model_validate_json(raw)
 except (json.JSONDecodeError, ValidationError) as e:
 if attempt < max_retries - 1:
 # Send error back to model and retry
 prompt += f"

Previous attempt failed: {e}
Fix and retry."
 else:
 raise

# Try it
contact = extract_contact("Reach out to Bob at bob@acme.com regarding the deal.")
print(f"Name: {contact.name}, Role: {contact.role}")

Tool use as structured output

# Pro tip: tool_use is FORCED structured output - cleanest approach
# Define a "tool" the model is forced to call, with your desired schema

extraction_tool = [{
 "name": "save_contact",
 "description": "Save extracted contact info.",
 "input_schema": {
 "type": "object",
 "properties": {
 "name": {"type": "string"},
 "email": {"type": "string"},
 "phone": {"type": "string"},
 "role": {"type": "string", "enum": ["customer", "lead", "vendor"]},

 },
 "required": ["name"],

}]

def extract_via_tool(text: str) -> dict:

 tool_choice={"type": "tool", "name": "save_contact"}, # FORCE this tool

Recipes by use case

  • Single field extraction: just ask for it; no JSON needed.
  • Few fields with optionals: JSON prefill works fine.
  • Strict schema, complex types: tool use + Pydantic.
  • Many records to extract: batch into one call with array output.
  • Provider-native modes: OpenAI 'response_format=json_schema'; Anthropic tool use; both pin output to schema.

If you can't measure your LLM system, you can't improve it. Building a proper eval harness — gold sets, metrics, regression tests — is what separates demos from products. This is also what lets you switch models or tweak prompts confidently.

What to measure

  • Correctness: did the output match expected? Use exact, fuzzy, or LLM-judge.
  • Faithfulness (for RAG): is the answer supported by retrieved context?
  • Format compliance: valid JSON, fields populated correctly.
  • Latency: p50, p95, p99 response times.
  • Cost: tokens per task, $ per 1000 requests.
  • Refusal rate: how often does the model decline?
  • User satisfaction: thumbs up/down, conversation length, escalations.

Running an evaluation

import time
from typing import Callable
from collections import defaultdict

def evaluate(system_fn: Callable, gold: list, scorer: Callable) -> dict:
 """system_fn(input_dict) -> output_dict; scorer(expected, actual) -> bool"""
 results = []
 by_tag = defaultdict(lambda: {"correct": 0, "total": 0})

 for ex in gold:
 t0 = time.time()
 try:
 actual = system_fn(ex["input"])
 ok = scorer(ex["expected"], actual)
 error = None
 except Exception as e:
 actual, ok, error = None, False, str(e)
 latency = time.time() - t0

 results.append({
 "id": ex["id"], "passed": ok,
 "expected": ex["expected"], "actual": actual,
 "latency": latency, "error": error,
 })
 for tag in ex.get("tags", ["_no_tag"]):
 by_tag[tag]["total"] += 1
 if ok: by_tag[tag]["correct"] += 1

 overall = sum(r["passed"] for r in results) / len(results)
 avg_latency = sum(r["latency"] for r in results) / len(results)

 return {
 "overall_accuracy": overall,
 "avg_latency_sec": avg_latency,
 "n_examples": len(results),
 "by_tag": {t: v["correct"]/v["total"] for t, v in by_tag.items()},
 "failures": [r for r in results if not r["passed"]],
 }

# Use it
def my_classifier(input_data):
 return classify_ticket(input_data["ticket"]) # from project 1

def category_match(expected, actual):
 return expected["category"] == actual.get("category")

eval_results = evaluate(my_classifier, load_gold(), category_match)
print(f"Accuracy: {eval_results['overall_accuracy']:.2%}")
print(f"By tag: {eval_results['by_tag']}")
print(f"Failures: {len(eval_results['failures'])}")

LLM-as-judge for open-ended outputs

# For tasks without a single right answer (summaries, explanations),
# use another LLM to score quality.

JUDGE_PROMPT = """You are evaluating the quality of an AI-generated answer.

Question: {question}
Reference answer: {reference}
Generated answer: {answer}

Rate the generated answer on:
- Correctness (1-5): factual alignment with reference
- Completeness (1-5): covers main points
- Clarity (1-5): well-written

Output JSON: {{"correctness": int, "completeness": int, "clarity": int, "notes": "..."}}"""

def llm_judge(question, reference, answer):
 r = client.messages.create(
 model="claude-haiku-4-5-20251001", max_tokens=300, temperature=0,
 messages=[{"role": "user",
 "content": JUDGE_PROMPT.format(
 question=question, reference=reference, answer=answer)},
 {"role": "assistant", "content": "{"}],
 stop_sequences=["}"],
 )
 return json.loads("{" + r.content[0].text + "}")

# Cautions:
# - Use a STRONGER model for judging than for the system being judged
# - Validate the judge with a small human-labeled set
# - Watch for biases: judges prefer longer answers, similar-style answers
# - Use multiple judges (different prompts/models) for important decisions

Eval-driven prompt iteration

  • Build the gold set BEFORE writing your prompt.
  • Make a baseline (e.g., naive prompt). Measure.
  • Iterate: change prompt → re-run eval → compare.
  • Track changes in a changelog. The 'why we added this example' note is gold.
  • Run evals automatically in CI before deploying prompt changes.
  • Continuously add examples from production failures.
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Don't optimize a single number. A prompt that hits 98% on your gold set might fail on novel inputs. Use a held-out test set, monitor production, and add adversarial examples (typos, mixed languages, edge cases). 'Gaming the eval' is one of the easiest ways to ship a worse system.

Page-aware chunking

import re

def chunk_with_provenance(pages: list[dict], chunk_size: int = 800,
 overlap: int = 100) -> list[dict]:
 """Each chunk knows what page it came from."""
 chunks = []
 for page in pages:
 text = re.sub(r"s+", " ", page["text"])
 # Split on sentence boundaries
 sentences = re.split(r"(?<=[.!?])s+", text)
 current, current_len = [], 0
 for s in sentences:
 if current_len + len(s) > chunk_size and current:
 chunks.append({
 "text": " ".join(current),
 "page": page["page"],
 })
 # Overlap: keep tail
 while current and sum(len(c) for c in current) > overlap:
 current.pop(0)
 current_len = sum(len(c) for c in current)
 current.append(s)
 current_len += len(s)
 if current:
 chunks.append({"text": " ".join(current), "page": page["page"]})
 return chunks

# Now each chunk has provenance: which page it came from

Indexing + retrieval with metadata

import chromadb
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

embedder = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")
chroma = chromadb.PersistentClient(path="./pdf_db")

def index_pdf(doc_id: str, path: str):
 collection = chroma.get_or_create_collection("pdfs")
 pages = parse_pdf(path)
 chunks = chunk_with_provenance(pages)

 # Embed in batches for speed
 embeddings = embedder.encode([c["text"] for c in chunks]).tolist()

 collection.add(
 ids=[f"{doc_id}_c{i}" for i in range(len(chunks))],
 embeddings=embeddings,
 documents=[c["text"] for c in chunks],
 metadatas=[{"doc_id": doc_id, "page": c["page"]} for c in chunks],
 )
 print(f"Indexed {len(chunks)} chunks from {len(pages)} pages")

def retrieve(query: str, doc_id: str = None, k: int = 5):
 collection = chroma.get_collection("pdfs")
 q_emb = embedder.encode(query).tolist()
 results = collection.query(
 query_embeddings=[q_emb],
 n_results=k,
 where={"doc_id": doc_id} if doc_id else None,
 )
 chunks = []
 for i, doc in enumerate(results["documents"][0]):
 chunks.append({
 "text": doc,
 "page": results["metadatas"][0][i]["page"],
 "doc_id": results["metadatas"][0][i]["doc_id"],
 })
 return chunks

Q&A with structured citations

from anthropic import Anthropic
from pydantic import BaseModel
from typing import List
import json
client = Anthropic()

class Citation(BaseModel):
 page: int
 quote: str # exact short snippet to support the answer

class Answer(BaseModel):
 answer: str
 citations: List[Citation]
 confidence: str # "high" | "medium" | "low" | "no_answer"

# Force structured output via tool use
qa_tool = [{
 "name": "submit_answer",
 "description": "Submit your answer with supporting citations.",
 "input_schema": Answer.model_json_schema(),
}]

QA_SYSTEM = """You answer questions using ONLY the provided context.

Rules:
1. Each claim must cite a specific page from the context.
2. Each citation needs a short EXACT quote from the source (5-15 words).
3. If the context doesn't answer the question, set confidence='no_answer'.
4. Don't invent facts. Don't generalize beyond the source.
"""

def answer_question(question: str, doc_id: str = None) -> Answer:
 chunks = retrieve(question, doc_id=doc_id, k=6)

 if not chunks:
 return Answer(answer="No relevant content found.",
 citations=[], confidence="no_answer")

 context = "

".join(
 f"[page {c['page']}]
{c['text']}" for c in chunks
 )
 prompt = f"""Context:
{context}

Question: {question}

Use submit_answer to respond."""

 r = client.messages.create(
 model="claude-haiku-4-5-20251001",
 max_tokens=1024, temperature=0,
 system=QA_SYSTEM, tools=qa_tool,
 tool_choice={"type": "tool", "name": "submit_answer"},
 messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
 )
 for block in r.content:
 if block.type == "tool_use":
 return Answer.model_validate(block.input)

 return Answer(answer="Failed to produce structured answer.",
 citations=[], confidence="no_answer")

# Try it
ans = answer_question("What is the company's refund policy?", doc_id="contract_v3")
print(ans.answer)
for c in ans.citations:
 print(f" Page {c.page}: "{c.quote}"")
print(f"Confidence: {ans.confidence}")

Verifying citations exist

# Citations are LLM-generated and can hallucinate
# Always verify each quoted snippet actually appears on the cited page.

def verify_citations(answer: Answer, doc_id: str) -> dict:
 collection = chroma.get_collection("pdfs")
 issues = []

 for cit in answer.citations:
 # Get all chunks from the cited page
 results = collection.get(
 where={"$and": [{"doc_id": doc_id}, {"page": cit.page}]}
 )
 page_text = " ".join(results["documents"]).lower()
 quote_lower = cit.quote.lower().strip()

 # Check exact match (or fuzzy)
 if quote_lower not in page_text:
 # Try simpler match - first 5 words
 short = " ".join(quote_lower.split()[:5])
 if short not in page_text:
 issues.append({
 "page": cit.page,
 "quote": cit.quote,
 "issue": "quote_not_found_on_page",
 })

 return {"verified": not issues, "issues": issues}

# Use it
ans = answer_question("What's the cancellation fee?", doc_id="contract_v3")
verification = verify_citations(ans, "contract_v3")
if not verification["verified"]:
 print("Warning: hallucinated citations:", verification["issues"])

Production polish

  • Page rendering: link from citation to a rendered page image so users can verify visually.
  • Reranking: after vector retrieval, use a reranker (Cohere Rerank, BGE Reranker) to re-score top-N. Big quality boost.
  • Multiple-doc Q&A: retrieve across all docs, group by doc, present clearly.
  • Conversation memory: build follow-up questions over prior answers.
  • Document ingestion pipeline: detect new uploads, parse, chunk, index automatically.
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Don't trust extracted PDF text blindly. PDFs frequently have: column-order issues (text reads zigzag), missing characters in fancy fonts, garbled tables, OCR errors on scanned docs. Always spot-check parsing output. For high-stakes use cases (legal, medical), use commercial parsers (Unstract, LlamaParse, Azure Form Recognizer).

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Code review is one of the highest-value uses of LLMs. A model can spot bugs, suggest improvements, check style, and explain unfamiliar code. This project pulls together everything from earlier chapters (prompt engineering, structured outputs, tool use) into a working assistant you can run on real diffs. The skills you build here apply directly to building automated PR reviewers, IDE plugins, and AI pair-programmers.

What we're building

A Python CLI tool that:

  1. Reads a git diff (or a single file)
  2. Sends it to an LLM with a code-review-specific prompt
  3. Parses the structured response (issues, severity, suggestions)
  4. Outputs a readable report

Project structure

code_reviewer/
├── reviewer.py        # main CLI entry point
├── prompts.py          # prompt templates
├── parser.py           # parse LLM output
├── git_helpers.py      # get diff, file content
├── tests/
│   └── test_reviewer.py
└── requirements.txt

Step 1: Get the code to review

# git_helpers.py
import subprocess

def get_staged_diff() -> str:
    """Return the diff of staged changes."""
    result = subprocess.run(
        ['git', 'diff', '--cached'],
        capture_output=True, text=True, check=True
    )
    return result.stdout

def get_file_content(path: str) -> str:
    with open(path) as f:
        return f.read()

Step 2: Write the prompt

# prompts.py
REVIEW_PROMPT = '''You are an expert code reviewer. Review the following code and identify issues.

For each issue, return a JSON object with:
- severity: one of "critical", "major", "minor", "nit"
- category: one of "bug", "security", "performance", "style", "readability"
- line: line number in the diff (or null if not specific)
- message: short explanation
- suggestion: optional concrete fix

Return your response as a JSON array. If there are no issues, return [].

Focus on REAL issues. Ignore style nits unless they significantly hurt readability.

CODE:
```
{code}
```

Output (JSON array only, no other text):'''

Key prompt-engineering decisions: (1) clear role assignment, (2) explicit schema, (3) emphasis on signal vs noise, (4) explicit output format constraint.

Step 3: Call the LLM

# reviewer.py
import anthropic
from prompts import REVIEW_PROMPT

client = anthropic.Anthropic()  # picks up ANTHROPIC_API_KEY env var

def review_code(code: str) -> str:
    response = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-sonnet-4-20250514",
        max_tokens=2048,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": REVIEW_PROMPT.format(code=code)}]
    )
    return response.content[0].text

Step 4: Parse the output

# parser.py
import json
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Optional

@dataclass
class Issue:
    severity: str
    category: str
    line: Optional[int]
    message: str
    suggestion: Optional[str]

def parse_review(raw: str) -> list[Issue]:
    # The model sometimes wraps JSON in code fences; strip them
    raw = raw.strip()
    if raw.startswith('```'):
        raw = raw.split('```')[1]
        if raw.startswith('json'):
            raw = raw[4:]
    
    try:
        data = json.loads(raw)
    except json.JSONDecodeError as e:
        raise ValueError(f"Model didn't return valid JSON: {e}\n\nGot: {raw[:200]}")
    
    return [Issue(**item) for item in data]

Step 5: Pretty-print the report

# reviewer.py (continued)
SEVERITY_COLORS = {
    'critical': '\033[91m',  # red
    'major':    '\033[93m',  # yellow
    'minor':    '\033[96m',  # cyan
    'nit':      '\033[90m',  # grey
}
RESET = '\033[0m'

def print_report(issues: list[Issue]) -> None:
    if not issues:
        print("✓ No issues found.")
        return
    
    # Sort by severity
    order = {'critical': 0, 'major': 1, 'minor': 2, 'nit': 3}
    issues.sort(key=lambda i: order.get(i.severity, 99))
    
    for i in issues:
        col = SEVERITY_COLORS.get(i.severity, '')
        line = f"line {i.line}" if i.line else "general"
        print(f"{col}[{i.severity.upper()}]{RESET} ({i.category}) {line}: {i.message}")
        if i.suggestion:
            print(f"    → {i.suggestion}")
        print()
    
    counts = {s: sum(1 for i in issues if i.severity == s) for s in order}
    summary = ", ".join(f"{n} {s}" for s, n in counts.items() if n > 0)
    print(f"Summary: {summary}")

Step 6: Wire up the CLI

# reviewer.py (continued)
import argparse
from git_helpers import get_staged_diff, get_file_content

def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="LLM-powered code reviewer")
    parser.add_argument("--file", help="Review a specific file")
    parser.add_argument("--staged", action="store_true", help="Review staged git changes")
    args = parser.parse_args()
    
    if args.staged:
        code = get_staged_diff()
        if not code.strip():
            print("No staged changes.")
            return
    elif args.file:
        code = get_file_content(args.file)
    else:
        parser.error("Need --file or --staged")
    
    raw = review_code(code)
    issues = parse_review(raw)
    print_report(issues)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Cost considerations

Each review call uses tokens. Estimate:

  • 1 KB of code ≈ 250 tokens input
  • Review response ≈ 200–500 tokens output
  • At ~$3/M input + $15/M output for Sonnet, a 5 KB diff costs ~$0.01

For a team committing 100 times per day, that's ~$1/day. Cheap. For very large diffs, batch them.

✓ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • A code-review assistant is mostly a well-designed prompt + structured JSON output
  • Decouple input (git diff) from output (formatted report) — easy to test and extend
  • Pre-commit hooks make the tool part of natural workflow
  • Always pretty-print with severity color-coding for human readers
  • Test the deterministic pieces (parser); mock the LLM in unit tests
  • Per-call cost is small; cache or batch for very large diffs
  • This project pulls together prompt engineering, JSON schemas, CLIs, and shell integration — a complete real-world LLM application

What you're building

A CLI tool that takes a Python file (or a Git diff) and produces a structured review: bugs, security issues, style problems, and concrete fix suggestions — each with severity and line references. This project teaches the two skills that separate toy LLM scripts from real tools: structured output you can trust and feeding the model the right context.

Step 1 — The review schema (design this FIRST)

REVIEW_SCHEMA = {
  "summary": "one-paragraph overall assessment",
  "issues": [
    {
      "severity": "critical | warning | style",
      "line": "int or null",
      "category": "bug | security | performance | readability",
      "description": "what's wrong",
      "suggestion": "concrete fix, with code if short"
    }
  ],
  "positives": ["things done well — reviews shouldn't only criticize"]
}

Step 2 — The prompt

SYSTEM = '''You are a senior Python reviewer. Analyze the code and respond
ONLY with JSON matching this schema: {schema}.
Rules:
- severity=critical only for actual bugs or security holes
- every issue MUST cite a line number from the numbered code
- suggestions must be specific (not "improve naming" but "rename d to days_elapsed")
- if the code is fine, say so — do not invent issues to seem thorough'''

def build_prompt(code: str) -> str:
    numbered = "\n".join(f"{i+1:4d} | {line}"
                          for i, line in enumerate(code.splitlines()))
    return f"Review this Python file:\n<code>\n{numbered}\n</code>"
# Numbering lines yourself = reliable line references in the output.

Step 3 — Robust parsing (the part everyone skips)

import json, re

def parse_review(raw: str) -> dict:
    # Models sometimes wrap JSON in ```json fences — strip them
    cleaned = re.sub(r"^```(json)?|```$", "", raw.strip(), flags=re.M).strip()
    try:
        review = json.loads(cleaned)
    except json.JSONDecodeError:
        # One repair attempt: ask the model to fix its own JSON
        review = json.loads(call_llm(f"Fix this into valid JSON, output only JSON:\n{cleaned}"))
    # Validate the contract
    assert "issues" in review and isinstance(review["issues"], list)
    for issue in review["issues"]:
        assert issue.get("severity") in ("critical", "warning", "style")
    return review

Step 4 — CLI with severity gating (CI-ready)

import sys, argparse, pathlib

def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("file")
    ap.add_argument("--fail-on", choices=["critical", "warning"], default=None)
    args = ap.parse_args()

    code = pathlib.Path(args.file).read_text()
    review = parse_review(call_llm(build_prompt(code)))

    for sev in ("critical", "warning", "style"):
        for i in [x for x in review["issues"] if x["severity"] == sev]:
            print(f"[{sev.upper():8}] line {i['line']}: {i['description']}")
            print(f"           fix: {i['suggestion']}\n")

    if args.fail_on:
        bad = {"critical": ("critical",), "warning": ("critical", "warning")}[args.fail_on]
        if any(i["severity"] in bad for i in review["issues"]):
            sys.exit(1)        # ← non-zero exit = CI pipeline fails the PR

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Extensions that make it portfolio-worthy

(1) Git-diff mode — review only changed lines: git diff main | python review.py --diff; this is how real review bots work. (2) Chunking — files over ~10k tokens get split by top-level functions/classes, reviewed per chunk, summaries merged. (3) GitHub Action — run on every PR, post the review as a comment, --fail-on critical. (4) Eval set — 10 files with KNOWN planted bugs; measure recall (bugs caught) and precision (non-bugs flagged) per prompt version, just like a model.

⚠ TRUST CALIBRATION

LLM reviewers are confidently wrong sometimes — they hallucinate issues in correct code and miss real race conditions. Position the tool as a FIRST-pass assistant that catches the easy 70%, never the final gate. The --fail-on flag should block on critical only, and humans review the criticals.

✓ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Schema first → prompt enforces it → parser validates it: the structured-output triangle
  • Number the lines yourself; strip code fences; one self-repair attempt on bad JSON
  • Non-zero exit codes turn any script into a CI gate
  • Evaluate the reviewer like a model: planted-bug recall and precision

Review hygiene: skip migrations and generated files — exclude them (globs like migrations/, *_pb2.py) from AI review and linting; humans didn’t write them and churn there is noise.

FastAPI service skeleton

# pip install fastapi uvicorn anthropic
from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException, Request
from pydantic import BaseModel
from anthropic import Anthropic, RateLimitError, APIError
import time, uuid, logging

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO,
 format="%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(message)s")
log = logging.getLogger(__name__)

app = FastAPI(title="LLM API", version="1.0")
client = Anthropic(timeout=30, max_retries=2)

class ChatRequest(BaseModel):
 message: str
 user_id: str
 conversation_id: str | None = None

class ChatResponse(BaseModel):
 answer: str
 request_id: str
 input_tokens: int
 output_tokens: int
 latency_ms: int
 cost_usd: float

# In production: use a real DB. For demo: in-memory.
conversations: dict[str, list] = {}

def estimate_cost(in_tok: int, out_tok: int) -> float:
 """Update with actual pricing for your model."""
 return in_tok * 1.0 / 1_000_000 + out_tok * 5.0 / 1_000_000

@app.post("/chat", response_model=ChatResponse)
async def chat(req: ChatRequest):
 request_id = str(uuid.uuid4())
 start = time.time()

 history = conversations.get(req.conversation_id or "", [])
 history.append({"role": "user", "content": req.message})

 try:
 r = client.messages.create(
 model="claude-haiku-4-5-20251001",
 max_tokens=1024,
 messages=history,
 )
 except RateLimitError:
 raise HTTPException(429, "Service is busy. Try again shortly.")
 except APIError as e:
 log.error(f"API error req={request_id}: {e}")
 raise HTTPException(503, "Upstream error.")

 answer = r.content[0].text
 history.append({"role": "assistant", "content": answer})
 if req.conversation_id:
 conversations[req.conversation_id] = history

 latency_ms = int((time.time() - start) * 1000)
 cost = estimate_cost(r.usage.input_tokens, r.usage.output_tokens)

 log.info(f"req={request_id} user={req.user_id} "
 f"tokens={r.usage.input_tokens}/{r.usage.output_tokens} "
 f"latency={latency_ms}ms cost=${cost:.4f}")

 return ChatResponse(
 answer=answer, request_id=request_id,
 input_tokens=r.usage.input_tokens,
 output_tokens=r.usage.output_tokens,
 latency_ms=latency_ms, cost_usd=cost,
 )

@app.get("/health")
async def health():
 return {"status": "ok"}

# Better: per-user quotas in Redis
import redis
r = redis.Redis()

def check_user_quota(user_id: str, daily_limit: int = 100) -> bool:
 key = f"quota:{user_id}:{time.strftime('%Y-%m-%d')}"
 used = r.incr(key)
 if used == 1:
 r.expire(key, 86400)
 return used <= daily_limit

# Cost-based limiting (more useful than request count)
def check_user_spend(user_id: str, daily_max_usd: float = 5.0) -> bool:
 key = f"spend:{user_id}:{time.strftime('%Y-%m-%d')}"
 spent = float(r.get(key) or 0)
 return spent < daily_max_usd

def record_spend(user_id: str, cost: float):
 key = f"spend:{user_id}:{time.strftime('%Y-%m-%d')}"
 r.incrbyfloat(key, cost)
 r.expire(key, 86400)

Caching for speed and cost

import hashlib, json, redis
r = redis.Redis(decode_responses=True)

def cache_key(model: str, messages: list, system: str = "") -> str:
 """Stable hash of the request."""
 payload = json.dumps({"m": model, "msgs": messages, "s": system}, sort_keys=True)
 return f"llm:{hashlib.sha256(payload.encode()).hexdigest()}"

def cached_completion(model, messages, system=None, ttl=3600):
 key = cache_key(model, messages, system or "")
 cached = r.get(key)
 if cached:
 log.info("cache_hit", key=key)
 return json.loads(cached)

 resp = client.messages.create(
 model=model, max_tokens=1024, system=system or "", messages=messages,
 )
 result = {
 "text": resp.content[0].text,
 "in_tokens": resp.usage.input_tokens,
 "out_tokens": resp.usage.output_tokens,
 }
 r.setex(key, ttl, json.dumps(result))
 return result

# Caching makes sense for:
# - Repeat queries (FAQ-style)
# - Idempotent extractions
# - Public/non-personalized responses

# Don't cache:
# - User-specific responses
# - Time-sensitive (weather, news)
# - Streaming responses (complicated)

# Provider-side prompt caching (different): Anthropic caches the prefix
# server-side, you pay much less for repeated prefixes - enable via cache_control

Background processing for heavy tasks

# Don't block HTTP for slow LLM calls. Use a queue.

from celery import Celery
celery_app = Celery("llm_tasks", broker="redis://localhost:6379/0",
 backend="redis://localhost:6379/1")

@celery_app.task(bind=True, max_retries=3, default_retry_delay=60)
def generate_report(self, user_id: str, params: dict):
 try:
 # Long-running multi-step LLM task
 # 30 sec, 10 LLM calls, etc.
 return {"status": "complete", "result": "..."}
 except Exception as e:
 self.retry(exc=e)

@app.post("/reports")
async def create_report(req: ReportRequest):
 task = generate_report.delay(req.user_id, req.params)
 return {"task_id": task.id, "status": "queued"}

@app.get("/reports/{task_id}")
async def get_report(task_id: str):
 task = generate_report.AsyncResult(task_id)
 if task.ready():
 return {"status": "complete", "result": task.result}
 return {"status": "pending"}

Production checklist

  • Secrets: never in code; use env vars or Secrets Manager. Rotate on exposure.
  • Authentication: protect endpoints; rate limit per user, not just IP.
  • Observability: structured logs, metrics (latency, errors, tokens, cost), traces.
  • Cost controls: per-user daily caps, alert on budget burn.
  • Rate limiting: 429s with Retry-After; protect upstream model.
  • Graceful degradation: cache, fallback to smaller model, queue overflow.
  • Versioning: pin model versions and prompt versions; test before rollout.
  • Privacy: minimize data sent to the LLM; redact PII; document retention policy.
  • Safety: content moderation on inputs and outputs; abuse detection.
  • Health/readiness checks: /health, /ready; orchestrator-friendly.
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

The single biggest production failure mode is uncapped spend. A bug in iteration logic, a malicious user, or an autoscaling event can burn $5,000 overnight. ALWAYS: per-user daily caps, total daily caps, billing alerts at the provider, monitoring on token rate. Treat LLM cost like database connections — finite, monitored, alarmed.

Practice

Add per-user daily token quotas to the chat endpoint using a simple in-memory dict. Reject requests after 10K input tokens/day with HTTP 429.

Show solution 
from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException
from pydantic import BaseModel
import time
from anthropic import Anthropic

app = FastAPI()
client = Anthropic()
quotas = {} # user_id -> {date: tokens_today}
DAILY_LIMIT = 10_000

def today():
 return time.strftime("%Y-%m-%d")

class Req(BaseModel):
 user_id: str
 message: str

@app.post("/chat")
def chat(req: Req):
 today_key = today()
 used = quotas.get(req.user_id, {}).get(today_key, 0)
 if used >= DAILY_LIMIT:
 raise HTTPException(429, f"Daily quota of {DAILY_LIMIT} tokens exceeded.")

 r = client.messages.create(
 model="claude-haiku-4-5-20251001", max_tokens=1024,
 messages=[{"role":"user","content":req.message}],
 )
 used += r.usage.input_tokens
 quotas.setdefault(req.user_id, {})[today_key] = used
 return {"answer": r.content[0].text, "used_today": used}

Key terms

FastAPI
Async Python web framework; ideal for LLM serving.
Rate limiting
Cap requests per IP/user/key.
Quota
Per-user daily limit on cost or tokens.
Caching
Local cache (Redis) and provider-side prompt caching.
Background queue
Celery/RQ for long tasks; don't block HTTP.
Observability
Logs + metrics + traces.
Graceful degradation
Smaller model fallback; cached response on outage.

Cost pattern: cache identical prompts — hash the prompt, check Redis before calling the API, store the response with a TTL; duplicate questions become free.

🧠 The Aistote Method (J-Method)

THE IDEA
The Aistote app is built on two of the most evidence-backed study techniques — active recall and spaced repetition — run in short, intense 25-minute blocks (its "J-Method"). Instead of slowly re-reading, you spend the time testing yourself and re-testing what you miss. This app already has every tool the method needs.
THE 3-STEP LOOP
StepWhat you doWhere in this app
1. ConvertTurn the material into questions instead of re-reading it.Open a section, skim the lesson once, then jump to its Quiz.
2. RecallAnswer from memory first — no peeking — then check.Take the section Quiz, or a PA / OA simulation; rate your confidence.
3. Space itRe-test only what you missed, on a growing schedule.Every miss becomes a Flashcard; review them on the app's spaced-repetition schedule.
A 25-MINUTE J-METHOD SESSION
TimeDo this
0–3 minSkim the lesson's key terms and the big idea — don't memorize yet, just get the lay of the land.
3–18 minTake the section quiz (or a 15-question drill). Try to recall the answer first, reveal it after.
18–23 minRedo only the questions you got wrong.
23–25 minSend the stubborn ones to Flashcards and note tomorrow's quick review.
Start the block with the ⚡ Focus timer (25 min) on any lesson — that is your J-Method session.
⚠️ THE ONE RULE
Always try to answer from memory before you look. The effort of retrieving is what actually builds the memory — re-reading feels productive but barely moves it.
WHY IT WORKS
Active recall (testing yourself) forces your brain to reconstruct the answer, which strengthens it far more than recognition. Spaced repetition reviews each fact just as you're about to forget it, moving it into long-term memory with the fewest reps. The 25-minute block simply makes you actually do both, every day.
DAILY RHYTHM
Two or three 25-minute J-Method blocks a day (new material in one, missed-question review in the next) beats a single long cram session — and it's how the Aistote method delivers "learn it in 25 minutes" instead of hours.

Choosing the Right Chart Type

The fundamental question: what is your data showing? — Before picking a chart, decide which of these you're trying to convey:

Comparison — Best for comparing a quantity across DISCRETE categories. Default to horizontal bars when category labels are long (they don't overlap).

Composition — Best for showing how subcategories add up to the total. Easy to compare totals across groups.

Distribution — For visualizing the distribution of ONE numeric variable. Choose bin count carefully — too few hides structure, too many is noisy.

Relationship — The default for showing relationship between two numeric variables.

Change over time — The standard for time series. Time on x-axis, value on y-axis, connecting line shows the trajectory.

Geographic — Coloring regions by value. Good for showing how a metric varies across states/counties/countries.
